name: AI Architect
role: Owns system shape: requirements to reference architecture, build/buy, governance, cost and risk. Day to day: ADRs, vendor bake-offs, security reviews, capacity models. Differs from AI Engineer (ships the app) and Infra (runs GPUs): you decide what gets built and why it survives a year.

subjects.title: Systems Thinking for AI Products
subjects.why: AI is a probabilistic subsystem; architecture must absorb that.
subjects.explainer:
Classical architecture assumes deterministic services. AI features return distributions, burn tokens, and fail semantically even when HTTP is 200. Your job is to place bounds: SLOs for latency and quality, human-in-the-loop where irreversible actions live, and clear ownership of model versus product metrics.

Decompose around bounded contexts, not around the newest framework. Prefer sync paths for user-facing chat and async workers for long agents. Design degraded modes (smaller model, cached answers, keyword search) the same way you design for AZ loss.

Common mistake: a single mega-agent diagram with no failure domains. Another: copying a Big Tech reference architecture that assumes their data platform.

Write ADRs that record the probabilistic assumptions — future you will need them when the model changes.

topics.title: Requirements

subtopics.title: Latency / accuracy / cost SLOs
subtopics.text: Give each user journey a latency target (for example p95), a quality target tied to an eval set, and a cost ceiling per request.

subtopics.title: Human-in-the-loop needs
subtopics.text: List the actions that are irreversible or high-impact and decide up front where a human must approve or review.

topics.explainer: AI requirements need numbers on more axes than usual. Besides features, pin down latency (time to first token and total), quality (task success on an eval set), cost per request or per user per month, and availability. Ask where data may be processed and stored, and whether tenants must be isolated. Decide where humans review or approve. Write abuse cases alongside use cases: what happens when someone tries to jailbreak it, scrape it, or run up the bill? Requirements that skip these show up later as surprise invoices, compliance blockers, or a security incident.

topics.title: Decomposition

subtopics.title: Sync vs async paths
subtopics.text: Interactive requests need answers in seconds; multi-step agents may run for minutes or days. Put the long work on queues with status updates instead of holding an HTTP connection.

subtopics.title: Degraded modes
subtopics.text: Decide what the user sees when the model is slow or failing: a cheaper model, a cached answer, a partial result, or a clear 'try later' message.

topics.explainer: Break the system along boundaries that fail and scale differently. Keep the synchronous user path thin and push slow work (enrichment, indexing, long agent runs) to async queues. Separate failure domains so a model provider outage degrades one feature instead of the whole product. Use strangler patterns to replace legacy flows incrementally rather than in a big bang. Design degraded modes up front: cached answers, a smaller fallback model, or a "we're busy, here's a form" path. A good decomposition makes it obvious which team owns which latency and cost budget.

topics.title: ADRs, teardowns and public benchmarks
topics.explainer: Architecture Decision Records are short documents: context, decision, alternatives considered, and consequences. Each one is numbered and immutable, and a later record supersedes it rather than editing it. Write ADRs for model choice, retrieval design and fallback policy. Public teardowns show a hiring manager how you think: the problem, the architecture, the eval results with numbers, the costs, what failed and what you would change. Publish reproducible benchmarks with the dataset, harness and settings so others can rerun them.

subtopics.title: ADR template: context, decision, consequences
subtopics.text: An ADR is a short note with context, the decision, alternatives considered and consequences. Keep them in the repo next to the code.

subtopics.title: Writing a system teardown
subtopics.text: A teardown explains a system you built or studied: the problem, the architecture, the eval numbers, the cost, what failed and what you would change.

quiz.q: A 200 OK from an LLM API guarantees…
quiz.why: Transport success is not task success.

quiz.q: Which is a non-functional requirement for an AI feature?
choices: p95 time to first token under 1 second
quiz.why: Latency targets constrain how, not what, the system does.

quiz.q: A degraded mode for an LLM feature could be…
choices: Serving a cached answer or a smaller fallback model
quiz.why: Planned degradation keeps users served when the main path fails.

quiz.q: How is an accepted ADR changed when the decision changes?
choices: Write a new ADR that supersedes it
quiz.why: ADRs are immutable; new records supersede old ones.

quiz.q: What makes a public benchmark credible?
choices: The dataset, harness and settings are published so others can reproduce it
quiz.why: Reproducibility is the bar.

lesson.intuition: A normal service either works or throws an error. An AI feature can return HTTP 200 with a confident, wrong answer. Systems thinking for AI means designing the whole product so that uncertainty is contained: you set quality targets, decide where humans check the work, plan what happens when the model is slow or down, and write down why you made each choice.
how: Write requirements in three columns: functional (what it does), non-functional (latency, cost, availability), and quality (accuracy on a named eval set).
Draw the data flow and mark every place where a model output becomes an action or a customer-visible answer.
Split the system into bounded contexts (for example intake, retrieval, generation, review) with clear owners.
Choose sync paths for interactive chat and async workers for long-running agents; give each a timeout and a degraded mode.
Record each important choice in an ADR so the next engineer knows the context and the alternatives.
lesson.example: Turning a vague goal into SLOs: 'answer HR questions well' becomes p95 latency ≤ 4 s, ≥ 90% correct on the 200-question golden set, cost ≤ $0.02 per question, and 99.5% monthly availability. At 50,000 questions a month the cost target caps spend at $1,000, which tells you which model tiers are even candidates.
mistakes: Treating the model as the product and skipping the surrounding workflow, review and fallback design.
Setting only latency and uptime SLOs and no quality SLO, so a silent accuracy drop never pages anyone.
Splitting into microservices by framework or vendor instead of by business capability.
lesson.enterprise: An insurer adds AI claim summaries. The architect keeps the claims system of record unchanged, adds an async summarization worker, shows summaries to adjusters with source links, and falls back to the old manual view if the worker is late. An ADR records why fully automatic decisions were ruled out.
takeaways: Design for 'wrong but confident', not just 'down'.
Quality needs an SLO and an owner, like latency.
ADRs make decisions reviewable and reversible.

subjects.title: ML / LLM System Lifecycle
subjects.why: Know data to production so you do not design dead ends.
subjects.explainer:
Hidden Technical Debt in ML Systems still applies — only now prompts, tools, and indexes are also config. Map data, train or adapt, eval, serve, monitor, feedback. Offline versus online features matter for classical ML; for LLMs the analogs are frozen corpora versus live retrieval and tool results.

Drift is not only statistical: prompt drift, schema drift, and harness drift break agents. Shadow and canary deployments need quality gates, not only error-rate gates.

Common mistake: treating the prompt store as tribal knowledge in Slack. Another: no owner for evaluation when the model vendor ships a silent upgrade.

Architects insist on lineage: which prompt, which index build, which model revision produced this answer.

topics.title: Pipeline

subtopics.title: Data to adapt to eval to serve to monitor
Offline vs online signals
subtopics.text: Offline signals come from fixed eval sets before release; online signals come from live users after release. You need both because each misses things the other catches.

subtopics.title: Shadow / canary / blue-green
subtopics.text: Shadow runs the new version on real traffic without showing users; canary shows it to a small share; blue-green switches all traffic between two full environments.

subtopics.title: Artifact lineage
subtopics.text: Lineage records which data, prompt, model and index produced each output, so you can trace a bad answer to its cause.

topics.explainer: An AI system is a pipeline, not a model: data flows into adaptation (prompts, RAG indexes, fine-tunes), into evaluation, into serving, and into monitoring that feeds back into data. Offline signals (eval scores) and online signals (user behavior) must both exist. Release with shadow, canary or blue-green deployments, exactly as with code. Track lineage so every response can be traced to a prompt version, model version, index snapshot and config. Without lineage you cannot answer the most common incident question: what changed?

topics.title: Debt and Drift

subtopics.title: Prompt and config drift
subtopics.text: Small prompt edits, provider model updates or changed defaults can shift behavior. Pin versions and rerun evals when anything changes.

subtopics.title: Harness drift
subtopics.text: The agent harness (tool definitions, retries, parsing) changes too, and a harness bug can look like a model regression.

topics.explainer: AI systems accumulate unusual debt. Data drift shifts inputs; concept drift changes what the right answer is. Prompts and configs drift as people tweak them in production without review. Harness drift happens when the agent framework changes behavior underneath you. Glue code between models, retrievers and tools grows into a jungle with no tests. The fix is boring discipline: version prompts and configs like code, monitor input distributions, assign an owner to every metric, and schedule regular eval refreshes so the golden set still reflects real traffic.

quiz.q: Prompt changes should be…
quiz.why: Prompts are production config.

quiz.q: Lineage lets you answer…
choices: What prompt, model, index and config produced this response
quiz.why: Lineage links outputs to every versioned input.

quiz.q: Concept drift means…
choices: The correct answer for the same input changes over time
quiz.why: For example, policy or price changes make old answers wrong.

lesson.intuition: An ML system is a loop, not a model file. Data flows in, a model is trained or adapted, it is evaluated, served, watched in production, and what you learn flows back into data. For LLM apps the 'model' also includes prompts, tools, retrieval indexes and the agent harness, and each of those can drift or break the loop.
how: Version every artifact: data snapshots, prompts, tool schemas, model IDs, index builds and harness code.
Evaluate offline on golden sets before release, with gates on quality as well as errors.
Release with shadow traffic or canaries, comparing quality metrics against the current version.
Monitor online signals: user feedback, escalation rate, cost, latency and sampled quality scores.
Feed failures and feedback back into data and eval sets, closing the loop.
lesson.example: Canary math: send 5% of 200,000 daily requests (10,000) to a new prompt version. If the old version's escalation rate is 4% and the canary shows 5.5%, the difference of 1.5 points on 10,000 requests is about 6-7 standard errors (canary SE ≈ √(0.055×0.945/10,000) ≈ 0.0023), a clear regression worth rolling back.
mistakes: Treating prompts and retrieval configs as code you can change without versioning or evals.
Gating deploys only on error rates when the real risk is lower answer quality.
Having no one who owns the production quality metric.
lesson.enterprise: A retailer's product-search assistant degraded after a catalog schema change renamed fields used in retrieval. Lineage linking the index build to the schema version showed the cause within an hour, and a quality gate now blocks index builds whose retrieval recall drops.
takeaways: Prompts, tools and indexes are model config: version them.
Gate releases on quality, not just errors.
Close the loop from production back to data.
lesson.diagram:
flowchart LR
  DATA[Data] --> ADAPT[Train / adapt / prompt]
  ADAPT --> EVAL[Offline eval gate]
  EVAL --> SERVE[Shadow / canary / serve]
  SERVE --> MON[Monitor]
  MON --> FB[Feedback + failures]
  FB --> DATA
lesson.diagramAlt: Diagram: a loop from data to adaptation, offline eval gate, serving with shadow or canary, monitoring and feedback back to data.
lesson.code:
# A minimal LLM-feature lifecycle as a pipeline definition (illustrative schema)
feature: support-answering
stages:
  - name: offline-eval
    gate: {golden_set: evals/support_v3.jsonl, min_pass_rate: 0.90}
  - name: shadow
    traffic_percent: 0          # mirror traffic, don't show users
    duration: 3d
  - name: canary
    traffic_percent: 5
    rollback_if: {error_rate: ">2%", p95_latency_ms: ">4000", judge_score: "<0.85"}
  - name: ga
monitoring: [cost_per_resolution, deflection_rate, thumbs_down_rate, drift_alerts]

subjects.title: Model Landscape Literacy for Architects
subjects.why: You cannot choose platforms without knowing model shapes.
subjects.explainer:
Frontier APIs, open-weight dense models, MoE, small on-device models, and VLMs are different animals for cost, control, and failure modes. Licensing (open weights versus open source versus proprietary API) constrains commercialization. Context length, tool-calling quality, and multilingual fertility change the architecture more than brand names.

Common mistake: picking a model from a leaderboard without matching the client's data residency and latency envelope. Another: ignoring tokenizer and chat-template lock-in when planning multi-vendor routing.

Keep a living scorecard: capability, controllability, cost, compliance, community.

topics.title: Model Types

subtopics.title: Open-weight dense
subtopics.text: Open-weight dense models give full control and can be fine-tuned and hosted anywhere, at the cost of running the serving stack yourself.

subtopics.title: SLMs / on-device
subtopics.text: Small language models (roughly 1-10B parameters) can run on a laptop, phone or single GPU, which helps privacy and latency for narrow tasks.

topics.explainer: Know the categories. Frontier APIs give top capability with no ops burden but less control over data, versions and cost. Open-weight dense models can be self-hosted and tuned, at the cost of running GPUs. MoE models give big-model quality with smaller compute per token but large memory footprints. Small language models run cheaply on CPUs, phones and edge boxes for narrow tasks. Vision-language and speech models add modalities with their own latency and cost profiles. Most real architectures mix several of these behind one gateway.

topics.title: Selection

subtopics.title: Leaderboard skepticism
subtopics.text: Leaderboards measure general tasks, may be contaminated, and rarely match your domain. Use them only to shortlist.

subtopics.title: Licensing and use rights
subtopics.text: 'Open weights' does not always mean open source: check the license for commercial-use limits, user thresholds and attribution rules.

subtopics.title: Eval on YOUR data
subtopics.text: Build a small, representative eval set from real tasks and run every candidate on it before deciding.

topics.explainer: Leaderboards are a starting filter, not an answer: benchmarks leak into training data and rarely match your domain. Read licenses carefully, since "open weights" may still restrict commercial use or user counts. Tokenizer and chat template choices create quiet lock-in in prompts and fine-tunes. Check tool-calling and structured output maturity if you are building agents. The only reliable selection method is running two or three candidates on your own golden set and comparing quality, latency and cost per successful task.

quiz.q: Open weights always means…
choices: Not automatically OSI open source or unlimited commercial rights
quiz.why: Weights, license, and API product are distinct.

quiz.q: The most reliable way to choose a model for a client is…
choices: Running candidates on the client's own golden set
quiz.why: Your data and tasks decide; benchmarks are only a filter.

quiz.q: Small language models are a good fit for…
quiz.why: They trade breadth for cost, latency and privacy.

lesson.intuition: Choosing a model is like choosing a vehicle. A frontier API is a rental supercar: powerful, no maintenance, but you follow the rental rules. An open-weight model is a car you own: you control it and can tune it, but you maintain it. Small models are scooters: cheap and fast for short trips. Architects need to know these shapes, not memorize leaderboard positions.
how: List the hard constraints first: data residency, latency, budget, license and deployment location.
Shortlist candidates of the right shape: frontier API, managed open model, self-hosted dense or MoE, small or on-device model.
Check practical fit: context length, tool-calling reliability, multilingual tokenization cost, structured-output support.
Evaluate the shortlist on your own task data and compare quality, latency and cost per correct answer.
Plan for change: keep prompts and evals portable so you can switch models later.
lesson.example: Cost per correct answer: Model A costs $0.010 per request at 92% accuracy, so $0.010 / 0.92 ≈ $0.0109 per correct answer. Model B costs $0.002 at 85%, so ≈ $0.0024. B is about 4.6× cheaper per correct answer; whether the 7-point accuracy gap is acceptable depends on the cost of an error.
mistakes: Picking a model from a public leaderboard without testing on your own data.
Ignoring license terms that restrict commercial use or require attribution.
Forgetting that tokenizer and chat-template differences make prompts non-portable.
lesson.enterprise: A European bank needs EU-only processing. It shortlists an EU-region managed API and an open-weight model self-hosted in its data center, runs both on 500 internal questions, and picks the managed option for general use and the self-hosted one for the most sensitive documents.
takeaways: Constraints first, benchmarks second.
Compare cost per correct answer, not price per token.
Keep evals portable so the model is a replaceable part.

flowchart TD
  C[Constraints: residency, latency, budget, license] --> S[Shortlist by shape]
  S --> F[Frontier API]
  S --> O[Open-weight dense / MoE]
  S --> SM[Small / on-device]
  F --> E[Eval on your data]
  O --> E
  SM --> E
  E --> P[Pick + keep portable]

lesson.code:
# Shortlist models by hard constraints first, then by quality per dollar (numbers are placeholders you fill in).
models = [
  {"name": "frontier-large", "ctx": 200_000, "usd_per_mtok": 15.0, "quality": 0.92, "self_host": False},
  {"name": "mid-tier",       "ctx": 128_000, "usd_per_mtok": 3.0,  "quality": 0.86, "self_host": False},
  {"name": "open-8b",        "ctx": 128_000, "usd_per_mtok": 0.2,  "quality": 0.74, "self_host": True},
]
need = {"min_ctx": 100_000, "must_self_host": False, "min_quality": 0.80}
ok = [m for m in models if m["ctx"] >= need["min_ctx"] and m["quality"] >= need["min_quality"]
      and (m["self_host"] or not need["must_self_host"])]
for m in sorted(ok, key=lambda m: m["quality"] / m["usd_per_mtok"], reverse=True):
    print(m["name"], round(m["quality"] / m["usd_per_mtok"], 3))

subjects.title: Reference Architectures
subjects.why: Reuse proven shapes; do not invent a snowflake per client.
subjects.explainer:
Most enterprise AI systems are compositions of a few patterns: request/response LLM API, RAG with citations, batch enrichment, event-driven agent workers, and human review queues. Layer edge, API, orchestration, model gateway, and data carefully. Separate control plane (prompts, policies, evals) from data plane (tokens, embeddings, tool I/O).

Multi-region and multi-tenant designs need sticky considerations for prefix caches and per-tenant keys.

Common mistake: drawing microservices everywhere when a modular monolith with a model gateway would ship sooner. Another: no shared observability layer, so every squad invents tracing.

Your deliverable is a one-pager engineers can build from — not a slide museum.

topics.title: Patterns

subtopics.title: LLM API facade
subtopics.text: A facade gives every team one internal API for model calls, hiding provider differences and adding logging and limits.

subtopics.title: RAG plus citations
subtopics.text: RAG retrieves relevant passages and asks the model to answer only from them with citations, so users can check the source.

subtopics.title: Human review queues
subtopics.text: Low-confidence or high-risk outputs go to a queue where people approve, edit or reject them, and their decisions become training and eval data.

topics.explainer: A handful of patterns cover most AI products. An LLM API facade wraps providers behind your own interface. RAG with citations grounds answers in your documents. Batch enrichment runs models over large datasets offline for classification or extraction. Agent workers execute multi-step tasks from a queue with tools and budgets. Human review queues route low-confidence or high-risk outputs to people. Knowing these lets you sketch a credible architecture in a first client meeting and then adjust for their constraints.

topics.title: Layering

subtopics.title: Control vs data plane
subtopics.text: The control plane changes slowly and needs review (prompts, policies); the data plane handles every request and needs speed and scale.

subtopics.title: Multi-region failover
subtopics.text: For failover, replicate indexes and configs to the second region and test that traffic can move with acceptable quality.

topics.explainer: Draw AI systems in layers: edge (auth, rate limits), API, orchestration (prompts, agents, workflows), model (gateway, serving), and data (indexes, stores). Separate the control plane, where policies, routing rules, prompt versions and budgets live, from the data plane that handles requests. Plan multi-region failover for both models and indexes. Shared services such as identity, billing, observability and secrets should be reused, not rebuilt per feature. Clear layers make it easy to swap a model or vendor without rewriting the product.

quiz.q: Control plane for AI usually includes…
choices: Prompt registry, policies, evals, routing config
quiz.why: Control plane governs how models are used.

quiz.q: Separating control plane from data plane means…
choices: Policies and configs are managed apart from request handling
quiz.why: Policy changes then do not require redeploying request paths.

quiz.q: Which pattern best fits classifying 10 million records overnight?
quiz.why: Batch APIs and offline pipelines are cheaper and simpler for bulk work.

lesson.intuition: Most enterprise AI systems are built from a handful of reusable shapes, like rooms in a house plan. There is the simple API call, the search-and-answer system (RAG), the overnight batch job, the background agent worker and the human review queue. A reference architecture shows how these pieces connect so each team doesn't reinvent them.
how: Pick the pattern that matches the job: request/response, RAG with citations, batch enrichment, async agent worker or review queue.
Layer it: edge (auth, rate limits), API, orchestration, model gateway, data and tools.
Separate the control plane (prompts, policies, eval configs, routing rules) from the data plane (tokens, embeddings, tool I/O).
Add shared services once: identity, billing, observability, secrets.
Plan multi-region and multi-tenant behavior, including cache affinity and per-tenant keys.
lesson.example: Batch vs realtime: enriching 2 million product descriptions overnight with a batch API that is priced at 50% of the realtime rate (as OpenAI's and Anthropic's batch APIs are) halves the bill. At 500 tokens each and $2 per 1M tokens realtime, that is 1B tokens → $2,000 realtime vs $1,000 batch.
mistakes: Drawing a microservice for every box before the system has one working path.
Mixing control-plane changes (prompt edits) into data-plane deploys without review.
Ignoring that prefix caches are per replica, so random load balancing lowers cache hits.
lesson.enterprise: A telecom company standardizes on three blueprints (RAG assistant, batch enrichment, agent worker with review queue). New teams start from a template that already includes the gateway, tracing and evals, cutting time to first pilot from months to weeks.
takeaways: A few patterns cover most systems.
Keep control plane and data plane separate.
Templates spread good defaults faster than documents do.

subjects.title: Build vs Buy vs Host
subjects.why: Wrong call here burns months of runway.
subjects.explainer:
Decision dimensions: capability ceiling, latency and region, data control and sovereignty, unit economics, lock-in and exit. Options: frontier APIs, cloud managed (Bedrock, Azure AI Foundry, Vertex), open-weight self-host, and hybrid routing (cheap model with escalation).

Gateways like LiteLLM or custom routers buy portability but add an ops surface. Self-hosting shifts spend from tokens to GPUs, people, and reliability engineering.

Common mistake: self-hosting for 'savings' at low volume where APIs would be cheaper. Another: all-in on one vendor with no export path for prompts, evals, and traces.

Score options with explicit weights tied to the client's constraints — not your favorite stack.

topics.title: Dimensions

subtopics.title: Capability ceiling
subtopics.text: Some tasks need the strongest model available; others are solved well by a small model. Measure, don't assume.

subtopics.title: Unit economics
subtopics.text: Compare cost per task at realistic volume, including tokens, GPUs, storage, people and support.

topics.explainer: Compare options on five axes. Capability ceiling: can anything but a frontier model do the task? Latency and region: where must inference run? Sovereignty: can data or weights leave the boundary? Unit economics: what is the cost per successful task at expected volume? Lock-in and exit: how hard is it to switch providers? Score each option against these explicitly with the client so the decision survives a change of leadership or a price change.

topics.title: Options

subtopics.title: Cloud managed platforms
subtopics.text: Managed platforms such as Amazon Bedrock, Azure AI Foundry and Google Vertex AI offer many models with cloud identity, networking and compliance controls.

subtopics.title: Hybrid routing
subtopics.text: Hybrid routing sends easy requests to a cheap model and escalates hard ones, often cutting cost a lot with little quality loss.

subtopics.title: Gateway layers (LiteLLM etc.)
subtopics.text: A gateway such as LiteLLM gives one API across providers, plus keys, budgets and fallbacks, at the cost of one more service to run.

topics.explainer: The realistic menu is: frontier APIs, cloud-managed platforms (Bedrock, Vertex, Azure AI Foundry), self-hosted open weights on your GPUs, or a hybrid with routing. Hybrid is common: cheap or private traffic goes to a self-hosted model, hard queries go to a frontier API. A gateway layer (LiteLLM, Envoy AI Gateway, Kong, or a cloud gateway) gives one API, keys, budgets and fallbacks across all of them. Self-hosting only pays off above a utilization threshold, so do the math first.

quiz.q: Hybrid routing primarily optimizes…
choices: Cost/quality by sending easy work to cheaper models
quiz.why: Route by difficulty/risk to control spend.

quiz.q: Self-hosting open weights usually pays off when…
choices: You need the best frontier model
quiz.why: GPU cost is fixed per hour; high utilization drives down cost per token.

quiz.q: A gateway layer gives you…
choices: One API, central keys, budgets and fallbacks across providers
quiz.why: It decouples apps from providers.

lesson.intuition: Build vs buy vs host is the classic make-or-buy decision with a twist: model capability changes every few months. Buying an API gets you the best models now with no hardware. Using a cloud platform adds enterprise controls. Hosting open weights gives control and possibly lower unit cost, but you take on GPUs, on-call and upgrades. Many teams end up with a hybrid.
how: Score the dimensions: capability needed, latency and region, data control, unit economics at expected volume, and lock-in.
Price each option at low, expected and high volume, including people and reliability work for self-hosting.
Prototype on an API first to learn the task and build evals.
Move specific high-volume or sensitive workloads to self-hosting only when the numbers and controls justify it.
Put a gateway in front so you can route between options and exit a vendor.
lesson.example: Self-host crossover: an H100 at about $3 per hour costs ≈ $2,190 per month (730 h). If one GPU serves a model at a sustained 1,500 output tokens per second at 50% average utilization, that's ≈ 1.97B tokens a month, or ≈ $1.11 per 1M tokens before engineering time. Against an API price of $0.60 per 1M, the API wins; against $5 per 1M, self-hosting may win if volume is steady.
mistakes: Self-hosting for 'savings' at low volume, where idle GPUs and on-call cost more than the API.
Comparing list prices without counting engineering time, monitoring and upgrades.
Signing up for a single vendor with no gateway or exit plan.
lesson.enterprise: A software company uses a frontier API for its coding assistant but self-hosts a fine-tuned small model for a high-volume ticket classifier, where steady traffic keeps GPUs busy and the per-token cost is lower.
takeaways: Start on APIs, learn, then optimize.
Self-hosting pays only at high, steady utilization.
A gateway keeps the decision reversible.
lesson.diagram:
flowchart LR
  N[Need] --> D{Volume, control, latency}
  D -->|low volume, best quality| API[Frontier API]
  D -->|enterprise controls| CM[Cloud managed]
  D -->|high steady volume or sovereignty| SH[Self-host open weights]
  API --> GW[Gateway]
  CM --> GW
  SH --> GW
lesson.diagramAlt: Diagram: a need is routed by volume, control and latency to a frontier API, cloud-managed platform or self-hosted open weights, all behind one gateway.
lesson.code:
# Break-even between paying per token and self-hosting a GPU (inputs are assumptions to replace).
api_usd_per_mtok = 0.60          # blended API price
gpu_usd_per_hour = 2.50          # one rented GPU
gpu_tok_per_sec  = 1_500         # sustained throughput you measured, not a spec sheet
utilization      = 0.40          # real traffic is bursty
self_usd_per_mtok = gpu_usd_per_hour / (gpu_tok_per_sec * 3600 * utilization / 1e6)
print(f"self-host ${self_usd_per_mtok:.2f}/Mtok vs API ${api_usd_per_mtok:.2f}/Mtok")
for u in (0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8):
    print(f"util {u:.0%}: ${gpu_usd_per_hour / (gpu_tok_per_sec*3600*u/1e6):.2f}/Mtok")
# Add people, on-call and upgrades before deciding; utilization dominates.

subjects.title: Enterprise Data Platforms for AI
subjects.why: Most AI projects fail on data access, quality, and rights.
subjects.explainer:
Lakehouse/warehouse, vector and keyword indexes, catalogs, lineage, and quality monitors are the substrate. Rights (training versus inference use), PII/PHI, and freshness SLAs constrain design. Chunking and metadata standards are architectural decisions, not afterthoughts.

Common mistake: a pilot on a CSV export that cannot be refreshed in production. Another: embeddings of secrets that now live forever in a vector store.

Define data contracts for each retrieval slice before model selection.

resources.title: Databricks ML
resources.why: Databricks' AI platform overview: building, deploying, evaluating and governing agent systems on lakehouse data (Mosaic AI, Unity Catalog).

resources.title: Designing Machine Learning Systems
resources.why: Chip Huyen's book (O'Reilly, page gated): data, features, deployment, monitoring and continual learning, framed as iterative system design.

resources.title: Designing Data-Intensive Applications
resources.why: Kleppmann's DDIA (O'Reilly, page gated): reliability, replication, partitioning, transactions, and batch vs stream. The systems foundation under every RAG and agent platform.

subjects.project: Design a data contract and retrieval slice for one domain including PII handling.

topics.title: Platform

subtopics.title: Vector + keyword indexes
subtopics.text: Vector search finds meaning, keyword search finds exact terms like part numbers. Most production systems use both.

subtopics.title: Catalog, lineage, quality
subtopics.text: A catalog tells you what data exists and who owns it; lineage shows where it came from; quality monitors catch broken feeds.

topics.explainer: AI rides on the data platform. A lakehouse or warehouse holds governed source data. Retrieval needs both vector and keyword indexes, ideally fed from the same pipeline. A catalog with lineage and quality checks tells you where each chunk came from and whether it is fresh. Embedding stores must be versioned with the embedding model, because changing models means re-embedding everything. Think about access patterns early: per-user ACL filtering at query time is far easier if permissions are stored as chunk metadata from day one.

topics.title: Rights and Quality

subtopics.title: Licensing / training rights
subtopics.text: Contracts and licenses may allow using data to answer questions but not to train models. Record this per source.

subtopics.title: Chunking and metadata standards
subtopics.text: Agree on chunk size, overlap and required metadata (source, owner, date, permissions) so every team's index is compatible.

subtopics.title: Retention and deletion
subtopics.text: Retention rules and deletion requests must cover raw data, chunks, embeddings, caches and logs.

topics.explainer: Before data feeds a model, know whether you have the right to use it for that purpose, especially for training. Scan for PII, PHI and secrets before indexing. Set freshness SLAs so stale documents do not produce confident wrong answers. Standardize chunking and metadata (source, owner, ACL, timestamp) across teams. Plan deletion end to end: removing a source document must also remove its chunks, embeddings, cache entries and any derived summaries, or you will fail a right-to-erasure request.

quiz.q: Deleting a source document requires…
choices: Also deleting or regenerating derived embeddings/chunks
quiz.why: Derived indexes retain content unless purged.

quiz.q: Switching embedding models requires…
quiz.why: Vectors from different models are not comparable.

quiz.q: Per-user permission filtering in RAG is easiest when…
choices: ACLs are stored as chunk metadata
quiz.why: Filter at retrieval time using metadata, not in the prompt.

lesson.intuition: AI projects usually fail on data, not models. The model can only answer from what it can reach, and only safely if you know who may see what. An enterprise data platform for AI is the plumbing that makes data findable, fresh, permission-aware and legally usable, from the warehouse to the vector index.
how: Inventory sources and owners, and record usage rights (inference only, training allowed, restricted).
Land data in a governed platform (lakehouse or warehouse) with a catalog, lineage and quality checks.
Build retrieval slices: chunked text with metadata, permissions and freshness timestamps, in vector and keyword indexes.
Scan for PII, PHI and secrets before indexing; mask or exclude as policy requires.
Define data contracts and freshness SLAs for each slice, and wire deletes through to indexes.
lesson.example: Freshness SLA: a policy assistant must reflect policy changes within 24 hours. A nightly re-index at 02:00 meets that only if the job never fails; adding change-data-capture to re-embed edited documents within 15 minutes makes the SLA robust, with the nightly job as a backstop.
mistakes: Piloting on a one-off CSV export that can't be refreshed in production.
Embedding documents that contain secrets or personal data, which then persist in the vector store.
Ignoring document permissions, so the assistant shows users content they shouldn't see.
lesson.enterprise: A pharmaceutical company indexes standard operating procedures with metadata for site, version and effective date. Retrieval filters on the user's site and only the current version, and superseded documents are removed from the index within an hour of a new version being approved.
takeaways: Rights, permissions and freshness are design inputs.
Metadata is what makes retrieval filterable and auditable.
Deletion must reach every copy, including embeddings.
lesson.diagram:
flowchart LR
  SRC[Sources + owners] --> LAKE[Lakehouse / warehouse]
  LAKE --> CAT[Catalog, lineage, quality]
  LAKE --> SCAN[PII / secrets scan]
  SCAN --> CHUNK[Chunk + metadata + ACLs]
  CHUNK --> IDX[(Vector + keyword index)]
  IDX --> APP[AI apps]
lesson.diagramAlt: Diagram: sources land in a lakehouse with catalog and quality checks, are scanned for PII, chunked with metadata and permissions, indexed, and used by AI apps.
lesson.code:
-- Expose a governed, AI-ready view instead of raw tables: documented, filtered, PII-free.
CREATE VIEW ai.customer_tickets_v1 AS
SELECT t.ticket_id,
       t.created_at,
       t.product_area,
       t.status,
       t.resolution_text,            -- free text for retrieval
       c.segment                     -- no name / email / phone
FROM   support.tickets t
JOIN   crm.customers  c ON c.customer_id = t.customer_id
WHERE  t.created_at >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '2 years'
  AND  c.consent_ai_processing = TRUE;
COMMENT ON VIEW ai.customer_tickets_v1 IS 'Owner: support-data. Refresh: hourly. Allowed: RAG, analytics.';

subjects.title: Model Gateways, Semantic Cache & Routing
subjects.why: The gateway is where cost, policy, and portability meet.
subjects.explainer:
A model gateway centralizes auth, budgets, routing, fallbacks, and observability across providers. Semantic caching (embedding-similar prompt reuse) can slash cost for FAQs but risks stale or cross-tenant leaks if keyed poorly. Structured rate limits and circuit breakers protect both wallet and upstream SLAs.

Common mistake: caching on raw prompt strings only, missing near-duplicates — or worse, caching across tenants. Another: a gateway that rewrites prompts silently and breaks eval baselines.

Treat the gateway as a product with its own SLOs and audit log.

resources.title: LiteLLM
resources.why: LiteLLM: the open-source gateway/SDK that gives 100+ providers one OpenAI-format API, with spend tracking, budgets, fallbacks and an admin UI.

resources.title: OpenTelemetry
resources.why: OpenTelemetry docs: the vendor-neutral standard for traces, metrics and logs. Instrument gateways and agents once and send the data to any backend.

resources.title: AWS Bedrock
resources.why: Amazon Bedrock docs: foundation model access, Knowledge Bases, Agents, Guardrails, model evaluation and data automation. Check here for what is managed vs what you build.

subjects.project: Sketch a gateway: routes, cache key design, tenant isolation, and fallback chain.

topics.title: Gateway Features

subtopics.title: Fallbacks and hedges
subtopics.text: A fallback tries another model after an error. A hedge sends the same request to two backends and uses the first good answer, trading cost for lower tail latency.

subtopics.title: Policy hooks
subtopics.text: Policy hooks run before and after the call: block disallowed content, redact PII, enforce allowed models per app.

topics.explainer: A model gateway sits between apps and model providers. It normalizes APIs so apps call one interface, holds provider keys so apps never see them, and enforces per-team budgets and rate limits. It adds fallbacks (switch provider on errors) and hedging (send a second request if the first is slow). Policy hooks run PII redaction, prompt-injection screening or content filters on the way in and out. Every call emits a unified trace with tokens, cost and latency, which makes it the natural place to measure and govern AI usage.

topics.title: Semantic Cache

subtopics.title: Embedding similarity keys
subtopics.text: Embed the prompt and look for a stored prompt above a similarity threshold. Set the threshold with an eval, because too low returns wrong answers.

subtopics.title: Tenant isolation
subtopics.text: Include the tenant (and often the user's permissions) in the cache key so answers never cross boundaries.

subtopics.title: Bypass rules
subtopics.text: Skip the cache for personalized, time-sensitive or tool-using requests.

topics.explainer: A semantic cache returns a stored answer when a new prompt is close enough in embedding space to an old one. It can cut cost and latency sharply for FAQ-like traffic. The risks are wrong hits and leaks: the similarity threshold must be tuned on real pairs, keys must include tenant, model and prompt version, and TTLs must respect how fast the truth changes. Never share cache entries across tenants or permission levels. Provide bypass rules for personalized, time-sensitive or tool-using requests.

quiz.q: Semantic cache keys should…
choices: Include tenant and policy scope, not only text similarity
Be a global hash of the prompt alone
quiz.why: Isolation and policy beat naive similarity.

quiz.q: Hedging in a gateway means…
choices: Sending a backup request if the first is slow
quiz.why: Hedging trades some extra cost for lower tail latency.

quiz.q: Semantic cache entries must never be shared across…
quiz.why: Cross-tenant hits leak data.

lesson.intuition: A model gateway is the front desk for every model call in a company. Instead of each app holding its own API keys and retry logic, all calls go through one service that checks who you are, enforces budgets, picks a model, retries or falls back on errors, caches repeat answers and records a trace. It is where cost, policy and portability meet.
how: Apps call one internal API; the gateway authenticates the app and the end user.
The gateway applies policy: budgets, rate limits, allowed models, PII redaction.
It routes the request to a provider or model by rules or a classifier, with fallbacks on errors or timeouts.
A semantic cache can return a stored answer for a near-duplicate prompt, keyed per tenant.
Every call emits a trace with tokens, cost, latency and model version.
lesson.example: Semantic cache savings: an FAQ bot gets 100,000 questions a month; 40% are near-duplicates of earlier ones above a similarity threshold of 0.95. At $0.004 per uncached call, cost drops from $400 to $240 (60,000 × $0.004), minus a small embedding cost of about 100,000 × 50 tokens = 5M tokens, around $0.10 at $0.02 per 1M tokens.
mistakes: Caching on exact prompt strings only, missing near-duplicates.
Sharing a cache across tenants, which can leak one customer's answer to another.
Letting the gateway rewrite prompts silently, which breaks eval baselines.
lesson.enterprise: A consulting firm routes all internal AI usage through a gateway with per-department budgets. When one team's script loops and burns $3,000 in an hour, the budget cap stops it and an alert goes to the owner.
takeaways: One front door for keys, budgets, routing and traces.
Cache per tenant with TTLs and bypass rules.
Fallbacks and circuit breakers protect both wallet and uptime.
lesson.diagram:
flowchart LR
  APP[Apps] --> GW[Gateway: auth, budgets, policy]
  GW --> C{Semantic cache hit?}
  C -->|yes| APP
  C -->|no| R[Router]
  R --> P1[Provider A]
  R --> P2[Provider B]
  R --> P3[Self-hosted]
  GW --> TR[(Traces + cost)]
lesson.diagramAlt: Diagram: apps call a gateway that checks auth and budgets, then a semantic cache, then routes to provider A, provider B or a self-hosted model, logging traces and cost.

case.title: Navigating the LLM Landscape: Uber's Innovation with GenAI Gateway (Uber Engineering, Jul 2024)
case.summary: Uber's Michelangelo team built a single GenAI Gateway, a Go service, for more than 60 LLM use cases. It mirrors the OpenAI HTTP/JSON interface while routing to external vendors and Uber-hosted models. It adds a PII redactor that anonymizes requests before they go to vendors and restores the entities afterwards, plus auth, metrics and audit logs for cost attribution. At the time of writing it served about 30 customer teams and 16 million queries per month.
case.lesson: One OpenAI-compatible front door lets you add security review, PII handling, budgets and logging once, for every team. PII redaction has latency and quality costs that you need to measure.

subjects.title: Forward Deployed Engineering: Discovery to Production
subjects.why: FDEs turn ambiguous customer problems into running agentic systems inside messy enterprises; it is the fastest-growing AI engineering role in services and labs.
subjects.explainer:
A Forward Deployed Engineer (FDE) embeds with a customer, writes production code in their environment, and owns outcomes such as time-to-value, adoption and reliability, not slideware. 2026 postings from labs, hyperscalers and consultancies describe the same loop: discover the real workflow, scope a narrow high-value use case, prototype in days, harden to production in weeks, hand over to the customer's team, and feed field learnings back to the product.

The technical stack is the whole atlas in miniature: Python and APIs, RAG and tool calling, MCP servers into legacy systems, evals, identity and security reviews, CI/CD and observability. The differentiator is judgment under ambiguity: choosing the use case where data access, measurable value and risk tolerance line up, and saying no to the rest.

Common mistakes: building a flashy demo on sample data that dies at the security review; no success metric agreed up front; ignoring the people whose work changes; leaving no runbook so the system rots after you leave.

Mental model: an FDE is a startup CTO for one customer problem, with a deadline and someone else's infrastructure.

resources.title: a16z: Trading margin for moat — the FDE model
resources.why: a16z on 'services-led growth': AI vendors use forward-deployed engineers to set up the product and trade margin for moat. Context for FDE roles.

resources.title: The Mom Test (customer conversations)
resources.why: The Mom Test: ask customers about their past behavior, not your idea, so discovery interviews give real requirements instead of polite lies.

resources.title: Anthropic: Building effective agents
resources.why: Anthropic's widely cited guide: start simple, prefer workflows (prompt chaining, routing, parallelization, orchestrator-workers, evaluator-optimizer) before autonomous agents.

subjects.project: Run a mock engagement: interview a 'customer' (a friend or LLM role-play) about a real workflow, write a one-page scope with success metric and data access plan, build a working prototype on their real-shaped data in 3 days, then a production-readiness checklist (security, evals, monitoring, runbook, handover) and a 10-minute exec readout.

topics.title: Discovery and scoping
topics.explainer: Start with the workflow, not the model. Shadow the people doing the work, map steps, systems, hand-offs and pain, and quantify volume and cost. Ask about past behavior, not hypothetical wishes. Then score candidate use cases on value, data accessibility, risk and measurability, and choose one narrow slice. Write a scope with a baseline metric, a target, the data and system access needed, the security reviewers, and what is explicitly out of scope. Getting access approved is often the critical path.

subtopics.title: Workflow shadowing and mapping
subtopics.text: Watch real people do the task and write down every step, system and hand-off. The real workflow usually differs from the documented one.

subtopics.title: Use-case scoring: value, data, risk
subtopics.text: Score use cases on business value, data availability and risk, then pick one that scores well on all three.

topics.title: Demo to production
topics.explainer: A demo proves possibility; production proves reliability. The path: prototype on real-shaped data, then build an eval set from customer examples, connect to real systems through least-privilege connectors, add tracing, guardrails and human approval for risky actions, pass the customer's security and privacy review, and roll out to a pilot group with feedback capture. Expect integration and data-readiness problems to consume most of the time, not prompting.

subtopics.title: Customer-derived eval sets
subtopics.text: Turn real customer examples, including tricky ones, into an eval set so 'is it good?' has a measurable answer.

subtopics.title: Integrations and identity
subtopics.text: Production means single sign-on, the customer's permissions and their systems of record, not a separate login.

topics.title: Handover, adoption and field feedback
topics.explainer: Success is the customer running it without you. Leave infrastructure as code, runbooks, dashboards, an eval suite and trained owners. Measure adoption and the business metric, not just uptime. Run enablement sessions and identify internal champions. Finally, codify what you learned into reusable patterns, connectors and product feedback, which is how FDE teams scale across many customers rather than rebuilding from scratch each time.

subtopics.title: Runbooks and ownership transfer
subtopics.text: Write down how to run, monitor and fix the system and who owns it, then rehearse with the customer team.

subtopics.title: Adoption and outcome metrics
subtopics.text: Track active users, tasks completed and the business metric, not just whether the system is up.

topics.title: Workshops, exec readouts and enterprise platform integration
topics.explainer: FDEs run discovery workshops: map the workflow on a whiteboard with the people who do it, list systems and data, and agree on the metric. Exec readouts are short: problem, result versus baseline, risks, cost and next step. Most enterprise value runs through SAP, Salesforce, ServiceNow, Workday and Microsoft 365, so learn their APIs, event models, permission schemes and the vendor's own agent features before building custom connectors.

subtopics.title: Discovery workshop format
subtopics.text: Run a short working session with the people who do the work: map the workflow, list systems and pain points, and agree on the metric.

subtopics.title: Exec readout structure
subtopics.text: Keep exec readouts to one page: problem, result versus baseline, risks, cost and the decision you need.

quiz.q: What should an FDE agree with the customer before building?
choices: A baseline and target success metric plus data access plan
quiz.why: Without a metric and access, the project cannot prove value or reach production.

quiz.q: What usually consumes most time between demo and production?
choices: Integration, data readiness and security review
quiz.why: Enterprise integration and approvals dominate real timelines.

quiz.q: What defines a successful FDE handover?
choices: The customer team operates it with runbooks, evals and dashboards
quiz.why: Ownership transfer is the goal.

lesson.intuition: A forward deployed engineer is part consultant, part software engineer. They sit with the customer, learn how the work really gets done, pick one valuable problem, and build a working system inside the customer's environment, not a slide deck. Success is measured by adoption and business results after they leave.
how: Discover: shadow the people doing the workflow, measure volume, time and error rates, and find the data and systems involved.
Scope: score candidate use cases on value, data readiness and risk, and agree on one success metric and baseline.
Prototype in days on real-shaped data, with a small eval set built from customer examples.
Harden in weeks: integrate with identity and systems of record, pass security review, add monitoring and human review.
Hand over: runbooks, training and ownership transfer; feed field learnings back to the product team.
lesson.example: Sizing a use case: 12 analysts each spend 6 hours a week preparing vendor-risk summaries, 72 hours a week in total. If an agent drafts summaries that cut that to 2 hours each, the saving is 48 hours a week; at a loaded cost of $90 per hour that's ≈ $4,320 a week, ≈ $225,000 a year, against an estimated run cost of $15,000 a year.
mistakes: Starting to build before agreeing on a measurable baseline and success metric.
Prototyping on clean sample data that looks nothing like production.
Leaving without a runbook or an owner, so the system decays after handover.
lesson.enterprise: An FDE at a logistics company maps the claims-dispute workflow, finds that 60% of time goes into gathering documents from three systems, and builds an agent that assembles a dispute packet for human review. Adoption is tracked weekly, and the customer's team owns it after eight weeks.
takeaways: Live in the workflow before you write code.
One metric, one baseline, one narrow use case first.
Handover and adoption are part of the job.
lesson.diagram:
flowchart LR
  D[Discover: shadow + measure] --> S[Scope: score use cases]
  S --> P[Prototype in days]
  P --> H[Harden in weeks]
  H --> HO[Handover + adoption]
  HO --> FB[Field feedback to product]
  FB -.-> D
lesson.diagramAlt: Diagram: the forward deployed engineering loop from discovery to scoping, prototype, hardening, handover and field feedback back to discovery.

subjects.title: FDE Discovery, Requirements and Scoping to an SOW
subjects.why: Most failed AI engagements fail at scoping: a vague goal, no baseline, no owner and no definition of done. A crisp statement of work with success metrics is the FDE's first deliverable.
subjects.explainer:
Discovery turns 'we want AI for support' into a scoped, measurable engagement. Shadow the workflow, map who does what and where the time goes, collect real examples (including the ugly ones), find the data and systems involved, and identify the economic buyer, the day-to-day owner and the blockers (security, legal, works council).

Then write it down as a statement of work (SOW): objectives, in-scope and out-of-scope items, deliverables, milestones, assumptions, customer dependencies, acceptance criteria tied to metrics with a baseline, and a change-control process. A good SOW protects both sides and makes the pilot's success provable.

resources.title: The Mom Test
resources.why: Rob Fitzpatrick's rules for customer conversations: talk about their life and past behaviour, not your idea. Essential for discovery interviews.

resources.title: HBR: Know Your Customers' 'Jobs to Be Done'
resources.why: Christensen, Hall, Dillon and Duncan explain how understanding the job a customer hires a product for makes innovation less hit-or-miss.

resources.title: Google: Rules of Machine Learning
resources.why: Martin Zinkevich's best practices, including launching with simple heuristics, designing and implementing metrics first, and choosing objectives you can measure.

resources.title: Anthropic: Building effective agents
resources.why: Helps scope the solution: start with the simplest workflow that meets the requirement, and add agentic autonomy only where it's needed.

subjects.project: Run a mock discovery for an 'AI support assistant': interview notes, a workflow map with time per step, 50 labelled example tickets, a stakeholder map, and a two-page SOW with baseline metrics, acceptance criteria and change control.

topics.title: Discovery that finds the real problem
topics.explainer: Customers describe solutions ('we need a chatbot'). Discovery finds the job behind them ('resolve password and billing tickets without an agent touching them'). Ask about past behaviour, not hypotheticals: what happened last week, how long it took, what it cost. Shadow the work and time each step. Collect 50–200 real examples, because they become your eval set. Map the systems (ticketing, CRM, knowledge base, identity) and the data each step uses. Map the people too: an executive sponsor with budget, a process owner, the users, IT and security, and anyone who can veto. End discovery with a written problem statement the sponsor agrees with.

subtopics.title: Jobs to be done
subtopics.text: Frame the goal as the outcome the user is trying to achieve, not the feature they asked for.

subtopics.title: Ask about past behaviour
subtopics.text: 'Walk me through the last time…' gives facts; 'would you use…' gives polite fiction.

subtopics.title: Workflow and time mapping
subtopics.text: Shadow users and time each step; the biggest time sink is usually the best first target.

subtopics.title: Stakeholder map
subtopics.text: Name the sponsor, owner, users, security reviewer and potential vetoes before writing a line of code.

topics.title: Scoping to a statement of work
topics.explainer: The SOW is the contract for the engagement's content. State the objective in one sentence with a metric, for example 'deflect 30% of tier-1 tickets at CSAT ≥ 4.2'. List deliverables, what is explicitly out of scope, milestones and dates, and the customer's dependencies (API access, SSO tenant, sample data, a named owner and response times). Record assumptions that, if false, change the plan. Define acceptance criteria as measurable thresholds against a baseline captured before the work starts. Add a change-control process so new requests become explicit trade-offs rather than silent scope creep.

subtopics.title: Objective and success metrics
subtopics.text: One outcome metric with a baseline and target, plus guardrail metrics such as CSAT, accuracy and cost.

subtopics.title: In scope and out of scope
subtopics.text: Explicit exclusions prevent the pilot from becoming a platform rebuild.

subtopics.title: Dependencies and assumptions
subtopics.text: Customer-owned prerequisites with dates; assumptions that trigger re-planning if false.

subtopics.title: Acceptance criteria and change control
subtopics.text: Measurable sign-off thresholds and a lightweight process for scope changes.

quiz.q: A customer says 'we need a chatbot'. Best discovery question?
choices: 'Walk me through the last 5 tickets your team handled and how long each took'
'How big should the context window be?'
quiz.why: Past behaviour reveals the real job and the baseline.

quiz.q: Which belongs in an SOW's acceptance criteria?
choices: 'Deflect ≥30% of tier-1 tickets with CSAT ≥4.2 over 4 weeks, versus the baseline'
quiz.why: Acceptance must be measurable against a baseline.

quiz.q: Mid-pilot, the customer asks to add Spanish support. What should happen?
choices: Run it through change control: assess impact, then agree to adjust scope, dates or price
quiz.why: Change control turns scope creep into an explicit trade-off.

lesson.intuition: Discovery is a doctor's appointment, not a sales demo. You ask what hurts, when it started and what was tried, and you run tests before prescribing. The SOW is the treatment plan both of you sign: what will be done, what won't, how you'll know it worked, and what happens if the symptoms change.
how: Interview about past behaviour and shadow the workflow; time each step.
Collect real examples and map systems, data and stakeholders.
Write a one-sentence objective with a baseline metric and target.
Draft the SOW: scope, exclusions, deliverables, milestones, dependencies, assumptions, acceptance criteria and change control.
Get the sponsor and owner to sign off before building.
lesson.example: Discovery at a 300-agent support centre: 42,000 tickets a month, average handle time 9.5 minutes, and 31% are 'where is my order' or password resets. The SOW objective: 'Resolve 25% of tier-1 tickets end to end with an AI assistant at CSAT ≥4.2 (baseline 4.3) within 8 weeks.' Acceptance is measured over 4 weeks on live traffic against the baseline period. The customer provides Zendesk API access, the Okta tenant and a named process owner by week 1. Out of scope: voice and non-English languages.
mistakes: Accepting the customer's solution ('a chatbot') as the requirement.
No baseline captured before work starts, so success can't be proven.
Missing out-of-scope list and change control.
Not identifying the security reviewer and other vetoes early.
lesson.enterprise: A global manufacturer's 'AI for procurement' request becomes, after two weeks of shadowing, a narrow SOW: classify and route incoming supplier invoices with exceptions to humans. With a baseline of 6.1 minutes per invoice and a named AP owner, the pilot has a clear finish line, unlike the previous vendor's open-ended proof of concept.
takeaways: Find the job behind the request through past behaviour and shadowing.
Real examples from discovery become the eval set.
An SOW needs a baselined metric, exclusions, dependencies and change control.
Map stakeholders and vetoes before you build.
lesson.diagram:
flowchart LR
  I["Interviews (past behaviour)"] --> W["Workflow + time map"]
  W --> EX["50-200 real examples"]
  W --> ST["Stakeholder + systems map"]
  EX --> BL["Baseline metrics"]
  ST --> SOW["SOW: objective, scope, exclusions, deliverables, dependencies, acceptance, change control"]
  BL --> SOW
  SOW --> SIGN["Sponsor + owner sign-off"]
lesson.diagramAlt: Discovery flow: interviews about past behaviour feed a workflow and time map, which produces real examples and a stakeholder and systems map. Examples give baseline metrics; together they feed an SOW covering objective, scope, exclusions, deliverables, dependencies, acceptance and change control, which the sponsor and owner sign off.

subjects.title: Security Architecture & Threat Modeling
subjects.why: Own the threat model before engineers write the loop.
subjects.explainer:
Assets include models, data, tools, and keys. Attack paths include indirect injection via retrieval, confused-deputy tool abuse, and supply-chain tampering of MCP servers. Map STRIDE-like analysis onto LLM apps; align with OWASP LLM Top 10 and ATLAS techniques.

Architectural controls: network isolation, sandboxes, tool allowlists, approval gates, vaulted secrets, immutable audits.

Common mistake: bolting a content filter on outputs while tools can still wire money. Another: shared service accounts for all agents.

Threat models are living documents — update when tools expand.

resources.title: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Apps
resources.why: OWASP's project page for the LLM Top 10: prompt injection, sensitive information disclosure, supply chain, excessive agency and more. A shared vocabulary for security reviews.

resources.title: MITRE ATLAS
resources.why: MITRE ATLAS: an ATT&CK-style knowledge base of adversary tactics and techniques against AI systems, with real-world case studies. Use it to name threats in a threat model.

resources.title: NIST AI RMF
resources.why: NIST's AI Risk Management Framework hub: the Govern/Map/Measure/Manage core, the playbook, translations and the Generative AI profile.

resources.title: Securing MCP (InfoQ)
resources.why: InfoQ article on defense-in-depth for MCP in production: four architectural layers, gateway-centered controls, authentication and tool vetting.

subjects.project: STRIDE-style threat model for an agent with email-read and ticket-write tools.

topics.title: Threat Modeling

subtopics.title: Indirect injection paths
subtopics.text: Instructions can arrive through any content the model reads: a retrieved page, an email, a file name, an image or a tool result.

subtopics.title: Confused deputy / tool abuse
subtopics.text: A confused deputy is a component with legitimate power that is tricked into using it for an attacker, which is exactly what a hijacked agent is.

topics.explainer: Start by listing assets: model weights, system prompts, training and retrieval data, tool credentials, user data. Then trace how untrusted text reaches the model, including indirect paths through documents, web pages, emails and tool outputs. The confused deputy is the key agent risk: the agent has permissions the attacker lacks and can be talked into using them. Add supply chain (models, packages, MCP servers) and abuse at scale (scraping, cost attacks). STRIDE still works; extend it with MITRE ATLAS and the OWASP LLM Top 10.

topics.title: Controls

subtopics.title: Tool allowlists / approvals
subtopics.text: Only allow tools, domains and recipients you have listed, and require approval for high-impact calls.

subtopics.title: Secrets vaulting
subtopics.text: Keep keys in a vault and give the agent short-lived, scoped tokens instead of raw secrets in its prompt or environment.

subtopics.title: Red-team cadence
subtopics.text: Schedule red-team exercises, for example each quarter and after big changes, and turn findings into regression tests.

topics.explainer: Controls that work regardless of model behavior: put tools and code execution in network-isolated sandboxes; use allowlists and human approvals for sensitive actions; keep secrets in a vault and inject short-lived, scoped tokens per call; log every prompt, tool call and approval in immutable storage; and schedule red-team exercises on a cadence, not once. Prefer architectural limits (the agent literally cannot reach the payments API) over prompt instructions (please don't touch payments).

quiz.q: A confused deputy in agent systems is often…
choices: A powerful tool identity abused via malicious instructions
quiz.why: Over-privileged tools act on injected instructions.

quiz.q: Which control is architectural rather than prompt-based?
choices: "Never reveal secrets" in the system prompt
Network policy that blocks the agent from the payments API
quiz.why: Architectural limits hold even when the model is tricked.

quiz.q: Which framework catalogs adversarial tactics against ML systems?
quiz.why: ATLAS extends ATT&CK-style tactics to AI systems.

lesson.intuition: Threat modeling is asking 'what could go wrong, and how bad would it be?' before you build. For AI systems the new twist is that the model reads untrusted text and can call tools, so an attacker who controls a document might control an action. A security architect maps assets, attackers and paths, then puts controls on the paths that matter most.
how: List assets: data, model weights, prompts, tools, credentials and logs.
List entry points for untrusted content: users, retrieved documents, web pages, emails, tool outputs, MCP servers.
Trace attack paths from each entry point to each sensitive asset or action (for example injection → email tool → data exfiltration).
Apply controls on the path: isolation, least privilege, allowlists, approval gates, vaulted secrets.
Log, monitor and red-team on a schedule, and update the model when the system changes.
lesson.example: Risk scoring: for each path, rate likelihood and impact 1-5 and multiply. 'Injection via shared drive document → email tool sends data outside' might be likelihood 4 × impact 5 = 20, top priority. 'Model weights stolen from internal registry' might be 2 × 4 = 8. Fixing the email path first (recipient allowlist plus approval) cuts its likelihood to 1, score 5.
mistakes: Adding an output content filter while tools can still move money or data.
Using one shared service account for all agent tools.
Threat modeling once at design time and never again after new tools are added.
lesson.enterprise: A bank's architect requires every agent tool to declare its data scope and side effects. Tools that send data externally need an allowlist and human approval; all tool calls are logged to an immutable store reviewed by the security team.
takeaways: Untrusted content + tools = attack path.
Control the capability, not just the prompt.
Re-run the threat model whenever tools change.
lesson.diagram:
flowchart LR
  IN[Untrusted inputs] --> M[Model / agent]
  M --> T1[Read tools]
  M --> T2[Write / send tools]
  T2 --> GATE{Allowlist + approval}
  GATE --> EXT[External systems]
  SEC[(Vaulted secrets)] -.scoped.-> T1
  SEC -.scoped.-> T2
  M --> AUD[(Immutable audit)]
lesson.diagramAlt: Diagram: untrusted inputs reach the agent, which uses read tools and write tools; write tools pass an allowlist and approval gate before external systems, with scoped secrets and an immutable audit log.
lesson.code:
# Lightweight STRIDE-style threat register for an agent, scored likelihood x impact.
threats = [
  ("Prompt injection via retrieved docs", "Tampering", 4, 4, "treat as data; no tool choice from docs"),
  ("Over-scoped API token",               "Elevation", 3, 5, "per-task scoped tokens"),
  ("PII in logs",                          "Info disclosure", 3, 4, "redact before logging"),
  ("Runaway tool loop",                    "DoS", 3, 3, "step and cost caps"),
]
for name, cat, l, i, ctl in sorted(threats, key=lambda t: t[2]*t[3], reverse=True):
    print(f"{l*i:>2}  {cat:<16} {name:<38} -> {ctl}")

subjects.title: Governance, Risk & Compliance
subjects.why: Enterprise deals die on GRC, not demos.
subjects.explainer:
EU AI Act risk tiers, NIST AI RMF functions, ISO 42001 AIMS, and sector rules (HIPAA, SOC2, FedRAMP) define the operating theater. Model cards, system cards, DPIAs, and human oversight roles are deliverables, not paperwork theater.

Common mistake: claiming 'we use OpenAI so we are compliant.' Another: no incident response playbook for model hallucinations that caused customer harm.

Architects translate legal tiers into technical controls and evidence packs.

resources.title: EU AI Act
resources.why: Independent EU AI Act site: the AI Act Explorer, a Compliance Checker, a high-level summary and a small business guide. Faster to navigate than EUR-Lex.

resources.title: NIST AI RMF
resources.why: NIST's AI Risk Management Framework hub: the Govern/Map/Measure/Manage core, the playbook, translations and the Generative AI profile.

resources.title: ISO/IEC 42001
resources.why: ISO/IEC 42001 (the ISO page blocked our fetcher): the certifiable AI management system standard covering policy, risk assessment, controls (Annex A) and continual improvement.

resources.title: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Apps
resources.why: OWASP's project page for the LLM Top 10: prompt injection, sensitive information disclosure, supply chain, excessive agency and more. A shared vocabulary for security reviews.

subjects.project: Classify a proposed system under EU AI Act tiers; draft a conformity checklist.

topics.title: Frameworks

subtopics.title: EU AI Act tiers
subtopics.text: The EU AI Act sorts uses into prohibited, high-risk, limited-risk (transparency duties) and minimal-risk, with separate rules for general-purpose AI models.

subtopics.title: NIST AI RMF
subtopics.text: NIST AI RMF organizes risk work into four functions: Govern, Map, Measure and Manage. It is voluntary but widely used.

subtopics.title: ISO 42001
subtopics.text: ISO/IEC 42001 is a certifiable management-system standard for AI, similar in style to ISO 27001 for security.

topics.explainer: The EU AI Act sorts systems into risk tiers, with heavy obligations for high-risk uses and transparency duties for general-purpose models. NIST AI RMF gives a voluntary govern-map-measure-manage structure widely used in the US. ISO/IEC 42001 is a certifiable AI management system standard, similar in spirit to ISO 27001. Sector rules (HIPAA, financial model risk guidance such as SR 11-7, and others) still apply. Contracts flow obligations down to vendors, so your model provider's terms become part of your compliance story.

topics.title: Operating Model

subtopics.title: DPIA / AI impact assessments
subtopics.text: An impact assessment describes the system, affected people, risks and mitigations before launch. GDPR requires a DPIA for high-risk personal-data processing.

subtopics.title: Incident response
subtopics.text: Define what counts as an AI incident, who is paged, how to contain it (for example disable a feature) and how to notify affected parties.

topics.explainer: Governance becomes real through artifacts and roles. Model and system cards document purpose, data, evals and limitations. AI impact assessments (often alongside DPIAs) record risks and mitigations before launch. Name who provides human oversight and what they can override. Extend incident response to cover AI failures such as harmful outputs, data leaks, or agent misbehavior. Keep evidence (eval results, approvals, change logs) organized so an auditor can follow it without a week of archaeology.

quiz.q: ISO 42001 is best described as…
quiz.why: 42001 is AIMS — management system for AI.

quiz.q: The EU AI Act primarily classifies systems by…
choices: Risk tier of the use case
quiz.why: Obligations scale with risk of the application.

quiz.q: NIST AI RMF's four functions are…
quiz.why: These structure AI risk work across the lifecycle.

lesson.intuition: Governance is how an organization proves its AI is used responsibly and legally. Regulations and standards such as the EU AI Act, the NIST AI Risk Management Framework and ISO/IEC 42001 say what must be true; the architect turns that into concrete controls, records and evidence that an auditor can check. Big deals are often won or lost here.
how: Classify each AI system by risk (for example under EU AI Act categories) and by sector rules.
Map required obligations to technical controls: logging, human oversight, data governance, accuracy testing, transparency notices.
Produce documentation: model or system cards, impact assessments (DPIA or AI impact assessment), and eval reports.
Assign roles: system owner, human overseers, incident responders.
Keep evidence continuously (logs, eval runs, approvals) so audits don't become a scramble.
lesson.example: Turning a requirement into controls: the EU AI Act requires high-risk systems to support human oversight and automatic logging of events. A loan pre-screening assistant implements this as (1) every recommendation shown to an officer who must approve or override, (2) a log of inputs, model version, output and the officer's decision kept for the retention period, and (3) a monthly report of override rates.
mistakes: Claiming compliance because the model vendor is compliant; obligations also apply to the deployer.
Treating documentation as a one-time task instead of keeping it current with each change.
Having no incident response plan for harmful AI outputs.
lesson.enterprise: A health insurer builds an 'evidence pack' per AI system: risk classification, model card, eval results by population group, human oversight procedure and incident log. Procurement reviews that used to take months now take weeks.
takeaways: Translate laws into controls and evidence.
Deployers have obligations too.
Collect evidence continuously.
lesson.diagram:
flowchart LR
  REG[Regulations + standards] --> CLS[Risk classification]
  CLS --> CTRL[Technical controls]
  CTRL --> DOC[Cards, assessments, eval reports]
  CTRL --> LOGS[(Logs + approvals)]
  DOC --> EV[Evidence pack]
  LOGS --> EV
  EV --> AUD[Auditors / customers]
lesson.diagramAlt: Diagram: regulations lead to risk classification and technical controls, which produce documentation and logs that form an evidence pack for auditors and customers.
lesson.code:
# AI use-case intake record (policy-as-data); fields map to risk tiers and required controls
use_case: hr-resume-screening
owner: talent-acquisition
risk_tier: high              # employment decisions are high-risk under EU AI Act Annex III
data: [resumes, job_descriptions]
human_oversight: required    # a recruiter makes every decision
controls:
  - bias_eval: quarterly
  - model_card: required
  - logging_retention_days: 365
  - user_notice: true
approvals: [legal, privacy, ai-review-board]

subjects.title: Cost Modeling & AI FinOps
subjects.why: Unit economics decide whether the architecture is viable.
subjects.explainer:
Model cost as dollars per million tokens in and out, cache hit savings, tool-call overhead, and GPU-hour TCO for self-host. Add egress, storage for indexes, and eval spend. Quotas, routing tiers, and batch versus realtime are architectural levers.

Common mistake: ignoring output tokens (often more expensive) or tool loops that multiply calls. Another: no chargeback, so every team treats the LLM budget as infinite.

Build a spreadsheet the CFO can read and the engineer can update.

resources.title: FinOps Foundation
resources.why: FinOps Foundation: framework, personas and maturity model for cloud financial management (inform, optimize, operate). The base vocabulary for AI cost work.

resources.title: AWS Bedrock
resources.why: Amazon Bedrock docs: foundation model access, Knowledge Bases, Agents, Guardrails, model evaluation and data automation. Check here for what is managed vs what you build.

resources.title: vLLM documentation
resources.why: vLLM docs (the site blocked our fetcher; content known from the project): install, OpenAI-compatible server, supported models, PagedAttention, quantization and distributed serving.

subjects.project: Spreadsheet: tokens in/out, cache hit rate, tool calls, GPU-hour alternative; find break-even.

topics.title: Unit Economics

subtopics.title: $/1M tokens in vs out
subtopics.text: Providers price input and output tokens separately, and output is usually 3-5× more expensive per token.

subtopics.title: Cache / prefix savings
subtopics.text: Prompt caching bills repeated prefixes at a steep discount, so put stable content (system prompt, tools, documents) first.

subtopics.title: GPU-hour TCO
subtopics.text: For self-hosting, total cost of ownership includes GPU rental or depreciation, power, networking, storage and staff time.

topics.explainer: Learn to compute cost per request: input tokens times input price plus output tokens times output price, with output typically 3 to 5 times more expensive. Prompt or prefix caching discounts repeated input heavily. For self-hosting, convert GPU-hour cost and measured throughput into dollars per million tokens. Do not forget egress, storage for logs and indexes, eval runs, and human review time, which can exceed model spend. The useful metric is cost per successful task, not cost per call.

topics.title: Controls

subtopics.title: Model routing tiers
subtopics.text: Send simple requests to cheaper models and escalate only hard ones.

subtopics.title: Batch vs realtime
subtopics.text: Batch APIs trade latency (results within hours) for roughly half the price, good for offline enrichment.

topics.explainer: Cost control is mostly architecture. Set per-tenant and per-feature budgets enforced at the gateway. Route easy queries to small models and escalate only when needed. Move anything that is not interactive to batch APIs, often half price. Show teams their spend (showback) or charge it back so incentives line up. Alert on anomalies such as a sudden jump in tokens per request, which usually means a prompt bug, a loop, or abuse.

quiz.q: Prefix caching helps most when…
choices: Many requests share a long stable prompt prefix
quiz.why: Shared prefixes make KV reuse pay off.

quiz.q: 1,000 input tokens at $3/M plus 500 output tokens at $15/M costs…
The best unit metric for AI cost is usually…
quiz.why: Failed or retried tasks hide in per-call numbers.

lesson.intuition: AI cost is a meter that runs on every token, tool call and GPU hour. A design that looks cheap in a demo can cost millions at scale because agents make many calls and output tokens cost more than input tokens. Cost modeling turns a design into dollars per task so you can compare options and set budgets before the bill arrives.
