how: Count tokens per task by stage: input, cached input, output, and number of calls per task.
Multiply by price per million tokens for each model, and add tool, embedding, storage, egress and eval costs.
Multiply by tasks per month for low, expected and high scenarios.
Apply levers: caching, routing to cheaper tiers, batch APIs, shorter outputs, fewer agent steps.
Set budgets and alerts per tenant and feature, with showback or chargeback.
lesson.example: Agent task cost: 6 model calls per task, each with 3,000 input and 400 output tokens. At $3 per 1M input and $15 per 1M output: input 18,000 × $3/M = $0.054, output 2,400 × $15/M = $0.036, total $0.090 per task. At 100,000 tasks a month that's $9,000. If 2,000 of each call's input tokens are a cached prefix billed at 10%, input drops to (6×1,000×$3 + 6×2,000×$0.30)/1M = $0.018 + $0.0036 = $0.0216, total ≈ $0.058 per task, ≈ $5,760 a month.
mistakes: Ignoring output tokens, which often cost several times more than input.
Pricing one call instead of a whole agent task with retries and tool loops.
No per-team budgets, so usage grows without anyone noticing.
lesson.enterprise: A media company's CFO asked why AI spend tripled. A cost model per feature showed one summarization feature re-sent the full article on every follow-up question; caching the article prefix and capping follow-ups cut that feature's cost by 55%.
takeaways: Model cost per task, not per call.
Output tokens and agent loops dominate.
Budgets and alerts belong in the design.
lesson.diagram:
flowchart LR
  T[Tokens per call] --> CALLS[× calls per task]
  CALLS --> PRICE[× price per 1M]
  PRICE --> OTHER[+ tools, embeddings, storage, evals]
  OTHER --> VOL[× tasks per month]
  VOL --> LEV[Levers: cache, route, batch, trim]
  LEV --> BUD[Budgets + alerts]
lesson.diagramAlt: Diagram: tokens per call times calls per task times price, plus other costs, times monthly volume, then cost levers and budgets.
lesson.code:
# Cost per resolved task, not cost per token.
price_in, price_out = 3.00, 15.00          # $ per million tokens (placeholder list prices)
calls_per_task, tok_in, tok_out = 4, 6_000, 700
cache_hit_rate, cached_discount = 0.5, 0.9 # share of input served from prompt cache, discount on it
eff_in = tok_in * (1 - cache_hit_rate * cached_discount)
per_call = (eff_in * price_in + tok_out * price_out) / 1e6
success_rate = 0.80
print(f"per call ${per_call:.4f}; per task ${per_call*calls_per_task:.4f}; "
      f"per SUCCESSFUL task ${per_call*calls_per_task/success_rate:.4f}")

subjects.title: Privacy, PII & Data Minimization
subjects.why: Privacy failures end deals and careers.
subjects.explainer:
Minimize what enters prompts and logs. Redact PII before tracing vendors. Prefer retrieval filters and field-level encryption over stuffing whole records. Understand training-use opt-outs on APIs versus self-host. Retention and right-to-be-forgotten must include vector indexes.

Common mistake: pasting production rows into a consumer ChatGPT account during debugging. Another: indefinite retention of session transcripts 'for quality.'

Privacy is an architecture constraint equal to latency.

resources.title: NIST AI RMF
resources.why: NIST's AI Risk Management Framework hub: the Govern/Map/Measure/Manage core, the playbook, translations and the Generative AI profile.

resources.title: EU AI Act
resources.why: Independent EU AI Act site: the AI Act Explorer, a Compliance Checker, a high-level summary and a small business guide. Faster to navigate than EUR-Lex.

resources.title: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Apps
resources.why: OWASP's project page for the LLM Top 10: prompt injection, sensitive information disclosure, supply chain, excessive agency and more. A shared vocabulary for security reviews.

subjects.project: Design a PII redaction path for prompts, tools, logs, and embeddings with deletion workflow.

topics.title: Minimization

subtopics.title: Prompt data minimization
subtopics.text: Include only the fields the task needs. A shipping-status answer needs the order ID and status, not the customer's full profile.

subtopics.title: Log redaction
subtopics.text: Mask personal data before it reaches logs and observability vendors, which often keep data longer and are accessed by more people.

subtopics.title: Training-use opt-out
subtopics.text: Check whether a provider may use your prompts for training, and turn that off by contract or setting if needed.

topics.explainer: The cheapest data to protect is data you never send. Strip or mask identifiers before prompts leave your boundary. Redact logs and traces by default. Apply field-level controls so the model sees only fields needed for the task. Review vendor data processing agreements for retention, training use and subprocessors, and turn off training-on-your-data where offered. Minimization reduces breach impact, regulatory scope and vendor risk all at once.

topics.title: Operations

subtopics.title: Index purge on delete
subtopics.text: When a record is deleted, also delete its chunks and embeddings and invalidate cached answers that used it.

subtopics.title: Regional processing
subtopics.text: Some laws and contracts require processing in a region. Choose endpoints, logs and backups in that region.

topics.explainer: Privacy is an ongoing operation. Set retention schedules for prompts, outputs and traces. When a user or document is deleted, purge it from indexes, caches and memories too. Review who can read raw logs and traces. Have a breach playbook that covers AI-specific leaks such as a model repeating another user's data. Respect data residency by pinning processing regions, including for embeddings and evals, not just the main model call.

quiz.q: Right-to-be-forgotten for RAG requires…
choices: Purging derived chunks/embeddings, not only the source row
quiz.why: Derived artifacts retain personal data.

quiz.q: Data minimization reduces…
choices: Breach impact, regulatory scope and vendor risk
quiz.why: Data never sent cannot leak.

quiz.q: Residency compliance must include…
choices: Embeddings, logs and evals as well
quiz.why: Any processing step can move data out of region.

lesson.intuition: Privacy by design means the safest personal data is the data you never send. AI systems tempt teams to paste whole records into prompts, log every conversation forever and index everything. A privacy-minded architecture sends only the fields a task needs, masks the rest, limits retention, and makes sure a deletion request reaches every copy, including vector indexes.
how: Identify personal and sensitive fields in each data source.
Minimize: select only the fields a task needs, and filter retrieval by the user's permissions.
Redact or tokenize PII before prompts, logs and third-party tracing tools where possible.
Review vendor terms: data processing agreements, training-use opt-outs, retention and region.
Operate: retention schedules, deletion that reaches indexes and caches, access reviews and breach playbooks.
lesson.example: Tokenization for prompts: a support message 'Hi, I'm Ana Silva, card 4111 1111 1111 1111, my refund is missing' becomes 'Hi, I'm [NAME_1], card [CARD_1], my refund is missing' before the model call. The model's reply 'Thanks [NAME_1]…' is re-identified in the app using a mapping stored only in the support system, so the model provider and logs never see the real values.
mistakes: Pasting production data into a consumer AI tool while debugging.
Keeping full conversation transcripts indefinitely 'for quality'.
Deleting a customer from the database but not from embeddings, caches or logs.
lesson.enterprise: A European retailer routes customer-service prompts through a redaction service, uses an EU-region model endpoint with training use disabled, keeps transcripts for 30 days, and runs a monthly job that verifies deleted customers no longer appear in any index.
takeaways: Send the minimum.
Redact before logs and vendors.
Deletion must reach every copy.
lesson.diagram:
flowchart LR
  SRC[Customer data] --> MIN[Select needed fields]
  MIN --> RED[Redact / tokenize PII]
  RED --> LLM[Model endpoint: region + no training]
  LLM --> REID[Re-identify in app]
  RED --> LOGS[(Redacted logs, short retention)]
  DEL[Deletion request] --> ALL[DB + index + cache + logs]
lesson.diagramAlt: Diagram: customer data is minimized and redacted before the model, re-identified in the app, logged in redacted form, and deletion requests reach the database, index, cache and logs.

case.title: LLM-powered data classification for data entities at scale (Grab Engineering)
case.summary: Grab uses LLMs to tag data entities (for example columns holding PII or other sensitive types) at scale, orchestrated by an internal service. That service is named Gemini, a name that predates Google's model.
case.lesson: Automated classification makes privacy controls scalable, but verify the tags and route uncertain ones to data owners.

subjects.title: AI Solutions Architecture: Sizing, Proposals and Build-vs-Buy
subjects.why: Solutions architects win and shape AI deals; credibility comes from realistic architectures, honest sizing and clear risk trade-offs.
subjects.explainer:
An AI Solutions Architect (pre-sales or delivery) translates a customer's goals into an agentic architecture, estimates cost and effort, and de-risks the decision. The work spans requirements and non-functional requirements, reference architectures (gateway, RAG, agents, data products, evals, guardrails, observability), platform choices (managed agent platforms vs frameworks vs custom), sizing (tokens per task × tasks per month × price; or GPUs for self-hosting), and a phased roadmap.

Strong architects make trade-offs explicit: managed APIs vs open-weight models for data residency; build vs buy for evals and observability; how much autonomy is acceptable at each phase. They write proposals that state assumptions, risks and success criteria, and they run proofs of value with eval-based exit criteria instead of vibes.

Common mistakes: costing only model tokens and forgetting retrieval, data engineering, evals and people; promising autonomy that the customer's risk appetite will not accept; vendor-locked designs with no exit path.

Mental model: a proposal is a hypothesis with a budget. Make the hypothesis testable.

resources.title: AWS Well-Architected Generative AI Lens
resources.why: AWS Well-Architected Generative AI Lens: questions and best practices across the six pillars, specific to generative AI workloads. Use it as a design-review checklist.

resources.title: Azure AI architecture center
resources.why: Azure Architecture Center hub for AI/ML: reference architectures for RAG and agents, AI landing-zone guidance and best practices to adapt to any cloud.

resources.title: Google Cloud architecture: generative AI
resources.why: Google Cloud architecture center for AI/ML: reference designs for generative AI, RAG and agent deployments on GCP.

subjects.project: For a mock RFP (e.g. insurer claims intake), produce a solution proposal: requirements and NFRs, reference architecture diagram, build-vs-buy table, monthly cost model at three volumes, phased roadmap with autonomy levels, risks and a proof-of-value plan with eval exit criteria.

topics.title: Requirements and reference architecture
topics.explainer: Capture functional goals and non-functional requirements early: latency, availability, data residency, privacy, auditability, languages, integration points and scale. Map them onto a reference architecture: channels, gateway, orchestration and agents, tools and MCP servers, data products and retrieval, eval and observability, policy and identity. Show where human oversight sits. Keep the diagram vendor-neutral first, then map components to the customer's cloud and existing tools.

subtopics.title: Functional and non-functional requirements
subtopics.text: Functional requirements say what the system does; non-functional ones cover latency, availability, security, residency and cost.

subtopics.title: Human oversight placement
subtopics.text: Mark exactly where humans approve, review or can override, because this shapes UX, staffing and compliance.

topics.title: Sizing and cost modeling
topics.explainer: Estimate tokens per task by stage (input context, outputs, tool loops), multiply by task volume and price per million tokens, and add retrieval, storage, data pipelines, observability, evals and human review. Compare managed APIs with self-hosted models at several volumes, because the crossover point drives architecture. Model people cost too: FDE time, operations and governance. Present ranges with assumptions, and the cost per business outcome such as cost per claim handled.

subtopics.title: Tokens per task by stage
subtopics.text: Estimate tokens for each step of the workflow (retrieve, draft, check), because multi-step agents multiply cost.

subtopics.title: API vs self-hosted crossover
subtopics.text: Self-hosting becomes cheaper only above a volume where GPUs stay busy. Compute that crossover explicitly.

topics.title: Proposals and proofs of value
topics.explainer: A good proposal states the problem, success criteria, architecture, phases, assumptions, risks, costs and what the customer must provide (data access, SMEs, approvals). A proof of value runs on the customer's data with a pre-agreed eval set and thresholds, timeboxed to weeks, with a go/no-go decision at the end. Include an exit path for vendor lock-in and a governance section that addresses their compliance needs.

subtopics.title: Proof-of-value design
subtopics.text: A proof of value uses real data, a time box and a pre-agreed metric so the result is a decision, not a demo.

subtopics.title: Lock-in and exit strategy
subtopics.text: Show how prompts, evals and data could move to another provider so the customer isn't locked in.

quiz.q: Which cost is most often forgotten in AI proposals?
choices: Data engineering, evals, operations and human review
quiz.why: Non-model costs often exceed token costs.

quiz.q: What makes a proof of value decisive?
choices: Pre-agreed eval set and thresholds on customer data
quiz.why: Agreed measurable criteria enable a real go/no-go.

quiz.q: Why compare APIs vs self-hosting at several volumes?
choices: The cost crossover point changes the right architecture
quiz.why: Economics change with scale.

lesson.intuition: A solutions architect turns a customer's goal into a credible plan: what to build, on which platform, how much it will cost and how risky it is. Customers have heard many AI promises, so credibility comes from honest sizing, a clear reference architecture and a proof-of-value with exit criteria agreed in advance.
how: Capture functional and non-functional requirements, including security, residency and oversight.
Map a vendor-neutral reference architecture (gateway, retrieval, agents, evals, guardrails, observability) onto the customer's cloud.
Size cost: tokens per task by stage × tasks per month × price, plus non-model costs; compare API vs self-hosting.
Design a proof of value with an eval set, success thresholds and a time box.
Write the proposal: phases, customer dependencies, risks, and an exit strategy from any vendor.
lesson.example: Sizing a document-review agent: 20,000 documents a month; per document, 8,000 input tokens and 1,000 output tokens across three steps. At $3/$15 per 1M: 160M input tokens → $480, 20M output tokens → $300, total $780 a month in model cost. Add ~$400 a month for search and hosting, so ≈ $1,180 a month, compared with an estimated 1,600 analyst hours a month today.
mistakes: Proposing a custom build when a managed platform or vendor feature would do.
Quoting only model cost and forgetting search, hosting, evals, monitoring and support.
Running a proof of concept with no agreed success criteria, so it never ends.
lesson.enterprise: For a manufacturer, an architect proposes a six-week proof of value: 300 historical maintenance tickets as the eval set, success defined as ≥ 80% correct root-cause suggestions, built on the customer's existing Azure tenancy, with a go/no-go meeting at week six.
takeaways: Honest sizing builds trust.
The eval set is the contract for the proof of value.
Always show the exit path.
lesson.diagram:
flowchart LR
  REQ[Requirements + NFRs] --> RA[Reference architecture]
  RA --> MAP[Map to customer cloud]
  MAP --> SIZE[Sizing + cost]
  SIZE --> POV[Proof of value + exit criteria]
  POV --> PROP[Proposal + roadmap]
lesson.diagramAlt: Diagram: requirements lead to a reference architecture, mapped to the customer's cloud, sized and costed, validated by a proof of value, and written up as a proposal and roadmap.
lesson.code:
# Size a deployment from traffic: peak concurrency via Little's law.
daily_requests = 200_000
peak_factor = 3.0                       # peak hour vs average hour
avg_latency_s = 6.0                     # end-to-end per request
rps_peak = daily_requests / 86_400 * peak_factor
concurrency = rps_peak * avg_latency_s  # L = lambda * W
per_replica = 32                        # concurrent sequences one replica sustains at SLO (measure it)
replicas = -(-concurrency // per_replica) + 1   # ceil + 1 for headroom/failover
print(f"peak {rps_peak:.1f} rps -> {concurrency:.0f} in flight -> {replicas:.0f} replicas")

subjects.title: Pilot to Production: Security Review, Data Residency and Procurement
subjects.why: Most enterprise AI pilots stall between 'the demo works' and 'it's in production'. The gate is security, legal and procurement, and FDEs who plan for it from day one ship.
subjects.explainer:
A pilot proves value on a small scope; production requires the organisation to accept the risk. Expect a security questionnaire (often based on SIG, CAIQ or a custom form), evidence such as a SOC 2 Type II report or ISO 27001 certificate, and an architecture review covering data flows, encryption, identity, logging and model-provider data use. Legal will want a DPA, data residency commitments and sometimes standard contractual clauses for transfers. Procurement brings vendor onboarding, insurance and pricing approvals.

Plan the gate from the start: collect evidence early, design for residency and zero data retention, and agree production criteria in the SOW.

resources.title: CSA Cloud Controls Matrix (CCM)
resources.why: CSA's cloud control framework: 197 control objectives in 17 domains, with the CAIQ questionnaire used in many vendor security reviews.

resources.title: AICPA: SOC suite of services
resources.why: AICPA's overview of System and Organization Controls reports, including SOC 2, the attestation most enterprise security teams request from SaaS vendors.

resources.title: European Commission: Standard Contractual Clauses
resources.why: The Commission's page on SCCs under the GDPR for transferring personal data from controllers or processors in the EU/EEA to third countries.

resources.title: AWS Well-Architected Generative AI Lens
resources.why: A production-readiness checklist across security, reliability, cost and operations for generative AI workloads. Useful structure for the readiness pack.

resources.title: OpenAI: Morgan Stanley customer story
resources.why: How evals, daily regression tests and zero data retention helped Morgan Stanley take advisor AI tools from pilot to firm-wide use with over 98% adoption.

subjects.project: Build a 'production readiness pack' for an AI assistant: data-flow diagram, completed CAIQ-style questionnaire, residency and retention design, eval report, runbook and rollback plan. Run a mock security review.

topics.title: Passing the security and architecture review
topics.explainer: Reviewers want to know what data goes where, who can access it and what happens when things go wrong. Bring a data-flow diagram that marks every system, region and trust boundary, including the model provider. Explain identity (SSO, SCIM, least-privilege service accounts), encryption in transit and at rest, key management, logging and retention, prompt-injection and data-exfiltration controls, and incident response. Have evidence ready: SOC 2 Type II report, penetration test summary, sub-processor list and the model provider's data-use terms (for example zero data retention). Answer questionnaires precisely; vague answers trigger follow-ups that cost weeks.

subtopics.title: Data-flow diagram
subtopics.text: Every hop, region and trust boundary, including model providers and logging.

subtopics.title: Evidence pack
subtopics.text: SOC 2 Type II or ISO 27001, pen-test summary, sub-processors and policies, ready before asked.

subtopics.title: Questionnaires (CAIQ, SIG)
subtopics.text: Standardized control questions; precise, consistent answers shorten review cycles.

subtopics.title: AI-specific controls
subtopics.text: Prompt-injection defences, output filtering, no training on customer data and human approval for risky actions.

topics.title: Residency, legal and procurement
topics.explainer: Data residency means data (and often processing) stays in a specified jurisdiction such as the EU. Design for it: regional deployments, regional model endpoints, regional logs and backups, and no silent cross-region fallbacks. Legal artefacts typically include a data processing agreement (DPA), a sub-processor list and, for EU-to-third-country transfers, standard contractual clauses. Procurement covers vendor risk onboarding, insurance, security addenda, pricing approval and sometimes an AI-specific risk assessment. Put these on the project plan in week 1 with owners on both sides, because they run on calendar time, not engineering time.

subtopics.title: Data residency by design
subtopics.text: Regional compute, model endpoints, storage, logs and backups, with tested failover inside the region.

subtopics.title: DPA and transfer mechanisms
subtopics.text: Data processing agreement, sub-processor list and SCCs when data leaves the EU/EEA.

subtopics.title: Procurement and vendor onboarding
subtopics.text: Vendor risk forms, insurance, pricing approval and contract redlines on a parallel track.

subtopics.title: Production criteria
subtopics.text: Agree go-live gates (eval thresholds, runbook, on-call, rollback) in the SOW, not at the end.

quiz.q: When should the security review start?
choices: In week 1, in parallel with the pilot build
quiz.why: Reviews take calendar time; starting late is the main reason pilots stall.

quiz.q: An EU customer requires residency. Which design detail most often breaks it?
choices: A silent fallback to a US model endpoint or US log storage
quiz.why: Fallbacks, logs and backups are where data quietly leaves the region.

quiz.q: What evidence do security teams most commonly ask a SaaS vendor for?
choices: A SOC 2 Type II report (or ISO 27001 certificate)
quiz.why: Independent attestation of controls is the standard starting point.

lesson.intuition: A pilot is a test drive; production is buying the car for the whole fleet. The test drive only needs a road and a driver. The fleet purchase needs inspections, insurance, a warranty and finance approval. FDEs who book the inspections on day one of the test drive are the ones whose cars actually get bought.
how: Agree production criteria (evals, security, residency, ops) in the SOW.
Start security, legal and procurement tracks in week 1 with named owners.
Produce a data-flow diagram and an evidence pack early.
Design residency, retention and model-provider data use explicitly.
Hold a go/no-go review against the agreed gates; ship with a runbook and rollback plan.
lesson.example: A 6-week pilot plan: weeks 1–6 build, while in parallel the security questionnaire (190 questions) is answered in week 1–2, the architecture review happens in week 3, the DPA and SCCs are negotiated in weeks 2–5 and procurement onboarding runs in weeks 1–4. Go/no-go is in week 6 against the gates: eval pass rate ≥ 0.9 on 300 cases, no high-risk findings open, EU-only data flows verified, runbook and on-call signed off. Starting these tracks at week 6 instead would typically add 8–12 weeks.
mistakes: Treating security review as a final step after the pilot.
Data-flow diagrams that omit the model provider, logs or backups.
Cross-region fallbacks that silently break residency commitments.
No agreed go-live gates, so 'production' is an endless negotiation.
lesson.enterprise: A healthcare network's pilot succeeded clinically but waited four months for review because the vendor couldn't say where prompts were logged. The next deployment led with a data-flow diagram, regional logging, a signed BAA and zero-retention model endpoints, and passed review in three weeks.
takeaways: Production is a risk decision; plan the gates from day one.
Bring a data-flow diagram and an evidence pack before you're asked.
Residency covers compute, model endpoints, logs and backups.
Run security, legal and procurement in parallel with the build.
lesson.diagram:
flowchart LR
  P["Pilot build (weeks 1-6)"] --> G{"Go / no-go gate"}
  S["Security questionnaire + architecture review"] --> G
  L["DPA, SCCs, residency design"] --> G
  PR["Procurement + vendor onboarding"] --> G
  E["Eval report vs SOW thresholds"] --> G
  G -->|"pass"| PROD["Production + runbook + on-call"]
  G -->|"fail"| FIX["Fix findings, re-review"]
lesson.diagramAlt: The pilot build runs in parallel with the security questionnaire and architecture review, legal work on the DPA, SCCs and residency, procurement onboarding, and an eval report. All feed a go/no-go gate; passing leads to production with a runbook and on-call, and failing leads to fixing findings and re-review.

case.title: Morgan Stanley uses AI evals to shape the future of financial services (OpenAI customer story)
case.summary: Morgan Stanley Wealth Management built an internal GPT-4 assistant for financial advisors and tested every AI use case with an evaluation framework before deployment, graded by advisors and prompt engineers. Daily regression tests of sample questions supported compliance, and OpenAI's zero data retention policy addressed the question of whether firm data would train public models. The firm reports over 98% adoption among advisor teams, with document access rising from 20% to 80%.
case.lesson: Evals plus clear answers to the data-use question are what move a pilot through risk review to firm-wide use. Adoption follows trust.

subjects.title: Enterprise Integration: SSO, VPN/On-Prem and SAP, Salesforce and ServiceNow
subjects.why: Agents create value only when they can read and act in the systems where work happens. In enterprises those are SSO-protected, often on-prem, and run on SAP, Salesforce and ServiceNow.
subjects.explainer:
Enterprise integration is a set of recurring problems. Identity: users sign in with corporate SSO (SAML or OIDC), are provisioned with SCIM, and agents call systems on their behalf with scoped tokens. Network: many systems sit on-prem or in private networks, reachable only through site-to-site VPN, private endpoints or an on-prem connector or agent that dials out. Systems of record: Salesforce (REST, Bulk and Streaming APIs), ServiceNow (Table API, Scripted REST, business rules and webhooks) and SAP (OData APIs via the SAP Business Accelerator Hub, often through SAP BTP).

Each has rate limits, permission models and change processes you must respect.

resources.title: Microsoft Entra ID: What is single sign-on?
resources.why: Microsoft's overview of SSO for enterprise apps in Entra ID, covering SAML, OpenID Connect and password-based options and how to choose between them.

resources.title: RFC 7644: SCIM protocol
resources.why: The HTTP protocol for System for Cross-domain Identity Management: creating, updating, deactivating and querying users and groups across domains.

resources.title: Azure VPN Gateway overview
resources.why: How a VPN gateway connects on-prem networks to cloud networks with IPsec/IKE site-to-site, VNet-to-VNet and point-to-site tunnels.

resources.title: SAP Business Accelerator Hub
resources.why: SAP's catalog of APIs (OData, SOAP, REST), pre-packaged integrations, business services and samples for S/4HANA and other SAP products.

resources.title: ServiceNow Table API (REST API reference)
resources.why: ServiceNow's documentation for the Table API, which performs create, read, update and delete operations on tables such as incident. (The page renders with JavaScript; the content is known from the docs.)

subjects.project: Design and prototype an integration map for a support assistant: Okta SSO and SCIM, a ServiceNow incident read/write tool, a Salesforce account lookup, an SAP order-status OData call through an on-prem connector, with scoped credentials and an audit log.

topics.title: Identity and network paths
topics.explainer: Start with identity, because everything else depends on it. Integrate the customer's IdP for user login, map groups to roles, and use SCIM for lifecycle. For system-to-system calls, prefer OAuth client credentials or on-behalf-of tokens with minimal scopes over shared passwords, and store secrets in a vault. Network paths come next. Cloud SaaS is reachable over the internet with IP allow-lists. Private systems need a site-to-site VPN, private connectivity such as PrivateLink or ExpressRoute, or an outbound-only on-prem connector, which security teams usually prefer because no inbound ports open. Document every path in the integration map.

subtopics.title: SSO and SCIM
subtopics.text: Corporate login via SAML or OIDC; automatic provisioning and deprovisioning via SCIM.

subtopics.title: Service identities and scopes
subtopics.text: OAuth client credentials or on-behalf-of tokens with least privilege; secrets in a vault, rotated.

subtopics.title: VPN and private connectivity
subtopics.text: Site-to-site IPsec VPN or private endpoints for systems not on the internet.

subtopics.title: Outbound-only connectors
subtopics.text: An agent or connector inside the network dials out to your service, so no inbound firewall holes are needed.

topics.title: Integrating systems of record
topics.explainer: Salesforce exposes REST and SOAP APIs, a Bulk API for large data loads and streaming events, with per-org API limits and object- and field-level security that your integration user inherits. ServiceNow's Table API reads and writes records such as incidents, and business rules or outbound REST messages can notify you of changes. SAP systems expose OData and SOAP services, discoverable in the SAP Business Accelerator Hub, often fronted by SAP BTP or an integration platform. Across all three: use a dedicated integration user with minimal permissions, respect API limits with backoff, write back through official APIs only, and log every agent action for audit.

subtopics.title: Salesforce APIs
subtopics.text: REST for records, Bulk for volume, Streaming or Change Data Capture for events; mind per-org API limits.

subtopics.title: ServiceNow Table API and events
subtopics.text: CRUD on tables such as incident; business rules and outbound REST for change notifications.

subtopics.title: SAP OData and BTP
subtopics.text: OData services described in the Business Accelerator Hub, often reached through BTP or middleware.

subtopics.title: Integration users and audit
subtopics.text: Dedicated least-privilege users per system, and an audit log of every read and write by the agent.

quiz.q: Security forbids opening inbound firewall ports to an on-prem SAP system. Common solution?
choices: An outbound-only connector inside the network that dials out to your service
Expose SAP directly to the internet
Disable the firewall during business hours
quiz.why: Outbound-only connectors avoid inbound exposure.

quiz.q: Your Salesforce integration hits API limits during a nightly sync. Better approach?
choices: Use the Bulk API or Change Data Capture instead of record-by-record REST calls
Create more integration users to bypass limits
quiz.why: Bulk and event APIs are designed for volume within limits.

quiz.q: How should an agent write a work note to a ServiceNow incident?
choices: Through the official Table API with a least-privilege integration user, logged for audit
With an admin password stored in the prompt
By screen-scraping the UI as an admin
quiz.why: Use supported APIs, least privilege and audit logging.

lesson.intuition: Integrating with an enterprise is like getting a contractor badge for a large office campus. First you need an identity (SSO), then a way in through the right gate (VPN or a connector), then permission to enter specific rooms (scoped integration users), and finally you must use the official forms in each department (SAP, Salesforce, ServiceNow APIs), with every visit signed in the logbook.
how: Draw the integration map: users, IdP, network paths, systems, data and actions.
Set up SSO, SCIM and scoped service identities first.
Choose network paths: SaaS over TLS with allow-lists, private systems via VPN, private endpoints or outbound connectors.
Build one tool per system action through official APIs, respecting limits and permissions.
Log every agent read and write, and test with the customer's admins.
lesson.example: A support assistant needs four integrations. Okta OIDC handles login, with SCIM for users. ServiceNow Table API reads incidents and writes work notes, as integration user svc_ai_triage with write access to only two fields. Salesforce REST looks up account tier, about 4,000 calls a day against a 100,000-call org limit. SAP order status comes from an S/4HANA OData service through an outbound connector in the customer's data centre. The integration map, scopes and audit log are in the security pack.
mistakes: Integration users with admin rights 'to save time'.
Opening inbound ports to on-prem systems instead of using outbound connectors or VPN.
Record-by-record API loops that exhaust Salesforce or ServiceNow limits.
Writing directly to databases or scraping UIs instead of using official APIs.
lesson.enterprise: A utility's field-ops assistant needed SAP PM work orders that lived on-prem. The customer's network team rejected a VPN into their core zone but approved an outbound connector in a DMZ, reaching three OData services with a read-only technical user. The integration map became the reference for two later AI projects.
takeaways: Identity first: SSO, SCIM and scoped service identities.
Pick a network path security can accept; outbound connectors are often easiest.
Use official APIs with least-privilege integration users and respect limits.
Audit every agent action across systems.

flowchart LR
  U["Employee"] -->|"SSO (SAML / OIDC)"| IDP["Okta / Entra"]
  IDP -->|"tokens + SCIM"| APP["AI assistant"]
  APP -->|"Table API, scoped user"| SN["ServiceNow"]
  APP -->|"REST / Bulk, scoped user"| SF["Salesforce"]
  APP <-->|"outbound connector"| CON["On-prem connector"]
  CON -->|"OData"| SAP["SAP S/4HANA (on-prem)"]
  APP --> AUD[("Audit log")]

The assistant calls ServiceNow's Table API and Salesforce REST or Bulk APIs with scoped users, reaches an on-prem SAP S/4HANA system over OData via an outbound connector, and writes every action to an audit log.

subjects.title: Multi-Region, Multi-Tenant, HA
subjects.why: Production AI must survive AZ loss and noisy neighbors.
subjects.explainer:
Tenancy isolation (keys, quotas, data partitions) prevents noisy-neighbor and leak disasters. HA needs RPO/RTO for model artifacts and indexes, traffic shifting, and degraded modes. Prefix-cache affinity can conflict with naive load balancing — design sticky or replicated caches deliberately.

Common mistake: active-active without index consistency story. Another: one GPU pool for all tenants with no fair-share.

Runbooks beat diagrams when pages fire at 3am.

resources.title: Google SRE Book
resources.why: Free Google SRE book: SLOs, error budgets, toil, monitoring, incident management, release engineering. Read chapters 4 and 6 before running AI in production.

resources.title: Azure AI architecture
resources.why: Azure Architecture Center hub for AI/ML: reference architectures for RAG and agents, AI landing-zone guidance and best practices to adapt to any cloud.

resources.title: K8s scheduling
resources.why: Kubernetes scheduling concepts: kube-scheduler, node affinity, taints and tolerations, pod priority and preemption. All of these matter for GPU placement.

subjects.project: Design active-active inference across two regions with failover runbook and degraded mode.

topics.title: Tenancy

subtopics.title: Noisy-neighbor isolation
subtopics.text: A noisy neighbor is a tenant whose load slows everyone else. Per-tenant quotas and queues prevent it.

subtopics.title: Cross-tenant cache risk
subtopics.text: A cache shared across tenants can return one customer's data to another. Namespace caches by tenant.

topics.explainer: Multi-tenant AI systems need isolation in places classic SaaS does not. One heavy tenant can saturate shared GPUs, so use quotas, fair queuing and priority classes. Give each tenant its own keys, budgets and rate limits. Partition data so retrieval filters by tenant at the index level, not in the prompt. Watch for cross-tenant leakage through shared semantic caches, shared memories or fine-tunes trained on mixed data.

topics.title: HA/DR

subtopics.title: RPO/RTO for model and index
subtopics.text: RPO is how much data you can lose (for example one hour of index updates); RTO is how long recovery may take.

subtopics.title: Traffic shifting
subtopics.text: Use DNS or global load balancers to move traffic between regions, and check that the target has capacity first.

subtopics.title: Game days
subtopics.text: A game day deliberately breaks something in a controlled way to test runbooks and alerts.

topics.explainer: Set RPO and RTO for every stateful part: model artifacts, vector indexes, prompt registries, conversation state. Replicate artifacts across regions ahead of time, since pulling 100+ GB of weights during an outage is slow. Use the gateway to shift traffic between regions and providers. Define degraded modes and practice failover in game days. A secondary provider with a different model also needs prompt and eval compatibility, or failover will quietly drop quality.

quiz.q: Sticky routing is sometimes needed to…
quiz.why: Cache locality can dominate latency and cost.

quiz.q: Noisy-neighbor protection on shared GPUs uses…
choices: Quotas, fair queuing and priority classes
quiz.why: These keep one tenant from starving others.

quiz.q: Why pre-replicate model weights to a DR region?
choices: Pulling 100+ GB during an outage is slow
quiz.why: Recovery time depends on artifacts already being there.

lesson.intuition: At scale, an AI service must keep working when a data center fails and when one big customer floods it with traffic. Multi-tenant design keeps customers isolated and fairly served; high availability keeps the service up and its indexes consistent across regions. It is classic distributed systems with some AI-specific twists, like GPU scarcity and prefix-cache affinity.
how: Isolate tenants: separate keys, quotas, data partitions and cache namespaces.
Share capacity fairly with per-tenant rate limits and weighted queues.
Set recovery targets (RPO and RTO) for model artifacts, indexes and configs, and replicate accordingly.
Plan traffic shifting between regions and degraded modes when capacity is short.
Practice failures with game days and keep runbooks current.
lesson.example: Fair share: a GPU pool serves 3,000 requests per minute. Tenant A sends 2,400 rpm, B 500 and C 300 (3,200 total). Without fair share, everyone queues. With equal weights, each tenant gets up to 1,000 rpm; B and C are fully served (800 total), and A gets the remaining 2,200 rpm, so only A is throttled by 200 rpm.
mistakes: Running active-active across regions with no plan for keeping indexes consistent.
One GPU pool with no per-tenant limits, so one customer can starve others.
Random load balancing that destroys prefix-cache hits.
lesson.enterprise: A SaaS vendor puts its largest customer on dedicated capacity, smaller ones on a shared pool with weighted fair queuing, and replicates vector indexes hourly to a second region with an RPO of one hour, tested quarterly.
takeaways: Isolation and fairness are product features.
Define RPO/RTO for indexes and models, not just databases.
Rehearse failover.
lesson.diagram:
flowchart LR
  TA[Tenant A] --> Q[Weighted fair queue]
  TB[Tenant B] --> Q
  TC[Tenant C] --> Q
  Q --> R1[Region 1 GPU pool]
  Q -. failover .-> R2[Region 2 GPU pool]

subjects.title: Internal AI Platforms
subjects.why: Scale the company by productizing plumbing once.
subjects.explainer:
An internal platform offers model gateway, prompt registry, shared evals, sandbox tool runtime, and cost dashboards as golden paths. Developer experience matters: templates, guardrail defaults, observability out of the box, clear chargeback.

Common mistake: a platform so rigid that squads shadow-IT another vendor. Another: a platform with no product owner — just tickets.

Measure adoption and time-to-first-eval, not only GPU utilization.

resources.why: Full Stack Deep Learning: courses and lectures on shipping ML and LLM products, including deployment, monitoring, UX and project management.

subjects.project: Sketch an internal AI platform: registry, eval harness, gateway, sandbox, cost view.

topics.title: Capabilities

subtopics.title: Prompt/version registry
subtopics.text: A prompt registry stores versioned prompts with owners and eval results, so changes are reviewed like code.

subtopics.title: Sandbox tool runtime
subtopics.text: A sandbox runs agent tools such as code execution in isolated containers with limited network and file access.

topics.explainer: An internal AI platform bundles the things every team would otherwise rebuild: a gateway with routing and budgets, a prompt and configuration registry with versions, a shared evaluation service, a sandboxed tool runtime for agents, and cost dashboards. The goal is that a product team can ship a safe, observable AI feature in days without becoming experts in GPUs or security.

topics.title: Developer Experience

subtopics.title: Golden paths
subtopics.text: A golden path is the easiest, supported way to build something, with good defaults already wired in.

subtopics.title: Self-serve vs ticketed
subtopics.text: Self-service lets teams start in minutes; tickets should be for exceptions like new providers or higher limits.

topics.explainer: Platforms succeed through developer experience. Offer golden paths: templates that come with auth, tracing, evals and guardrails already wired. Make safe defaults the easy path. Turn on observability automatically. Make costs visible per team. Prefer self-service with policy guardrails over ticket queues, because teams route around slow platforms and that is how shadow AI starts. Try it: time how long a new team takes from "we want an AI feature" to a traced, budgeted endpoint in staging. If it is weeks, that number is your platform roadmap.

quiz.q: A healthy AI platform optimizes for…
quiz.why: Enable safe speed.

quiz.q: A golden path is…
choices: A template with auth, tracing, evals and guardrails pre-wired
quiz.why: It makes the safe way the easy way.

quiz.q: Shadow AI usually grows when…
choices: The official platform is slow or ticket-driven
quiz.why: Teams route around friction.

lesson.intuition: An internal AI platform is a paved road. Instead of every team wiring up keys, evals, guardrails and dashboards on its own, the platform team builds them once and offers templates that are easy to adopt. Good platforms are treated as products with users, feedback and roadmaps, not as ticket queues.
how: Offer core services: model gateway, prompt and version registry, shared eval service, sandboxed tool runtime, cost dashboards.
Package them as golden paths: a template that gives a new app tracing, evals and guardrails by default.
Make self-service the default; reserve tickets for exceptions.
Show cost and usage per team so chargeback is clear.
Measure adoption and time to first eval, and run the platform like a product.
lesson.example: Time to first eval: before the platform, a new team needed about 3 weeks to set up keys, logging and an eval harness. With a template repo and shared eval service it takes 1 day. With 20 new AI projects a year, that saves about 20 × 14 working days ≈ 280 engineer-days.
mistakes: Building a platform so rigid that teams bypass it with their own vendor accounts.
No product owner, so the platform becomes a backlog of tickets.
Measuring only GPU utilization instead of developer adoption and outcomes.
lesson.enterprise: A large retailer's platform team offers a 'new AI app' template with gateway access, OpenTelemetry tracing and an eval CI job. Within a year 80% of AI projects use it, and security reviews are faster because defaults are already approved.
takeaways: Paved roads beat mandates.
Defaults (tracing, guardrails, evals) spread good practice.
Treat the platform as a product.

  TPL --> GW[Gateway]
  TPL --> REG[Prompt registry]
  TPL --> EVAL[Eval service]

case.title: Navigating the LLM Landscape: Uber's Innovation with GenAI Gateway (Uber Engineering, Jul 2024)
case.summary: Uber's Michelangelo team built a single GenAI Gateway, a Go service, for more than 60 LLM use cases. It mirrors the OpenAI HTTP/JSON interface while routing to external vendors and Uber-hosted models. It adds a PII redactor that anonymizes requests before they go to vendors and restores the entities afterwards, plus auth, metrics and audit logs for cost attribution. At the time of writing it served about 30 customer teams and 16 million queries per month.
case.lesson: One OpenAI-compatible front door lets you add security review, PII handling, budgets and logging once, for every team. PII redaction has latency and quality costs that you need to measure.

subjects.title: Model Cards, Licensing & Procurement
subjects.why: Paperwork is part of the architecture in regulated deals.
subjects.explainer:
Model cards and system cards communicate intended use, limits, and eval summaries. Licensing distinguishes API ToS, open weights, copyleft, and training-data provenance claims. Procurement needs security questionnaires, subprocessors, and exit clauses.

Common mistake: assuming Hugging Face hosting implies a particular license. Another: no plan to extract prompts and evals when switching vendors.

Keep a contract checklist next to the reference architecture.

resources.title: EU AI Act
resources.why: Independent EU AI Act site: the AI Act Explorer, a Compliance Checker, a high-level summary and a small business guide. Faster to navigate than EUR-Lex.

resources.title: NIST AI RMF
resources.why: NIST's AI Risk Management Framework hub: the Govern/Map/Measure/Manage core, the playbook, translations and the Generative AI profile.

resources.title: Hugging Face LLM Course
resources.why: Hugging Face's free LLM course: Transformers library basics, tokenizers, fine-tuning and sharing models on the Hub, with runnable notebooks.

subjects.project: Fill a model/system card for a client-facing RAG assistant; list license and exit risks.

topics.title: Documentation

subtopics.title: Model cards
subtopics.text: Model cards, introduced by Mitchell et al. in 2019, describe a model's intended use, training data, evaluation results and limitations.

subtopics.title: System cards
subtopics.text: A system card covers the whole application: model, prompts, tools, guardrails, human oversight and evals.

topics.explainer: Documentation is how trust scales. Model cards describe what a model is, how it was trained and evaluated, and where it fails. System cards describe the whole application, including prompts, tools, guardrails and human oversight. Publish eval summaries and known limitations honestly. Keep a change log of model and prompt versions so users and auditors can match behavior to releases.

topics.title: Procurement

subtopics.title: ToS vs weight licenses
subtopics.text: API terms of service govern hosted use; weight licenses govern downloaded models. Both may restrict use cases or require attribution.

subtopics.title: Exit and data return
subtopics.text: Contracts should say how you get your data, fine-tuned weights and logs back, and how fast the vendor deletes them.

topics.explainer: Procurement for AI has new details. API terms of service and open-weight licenses differ: check commercial use, user thresholds, and output ownership. List subprocessors and data locations. Prepare for security questionnaires that ask about training on customer data, retention, and isolation. Negotiate exit terms, including data return and deletion. Ask about indemnity for IP claims on outputs, and check whether your insurance covers AI-related incidents.

quiz.q: A model card should include…
choices: Intended use, limits, and evaluation notes
quiz.why: Cards communicate safe use boundaries.

quiz.q: A system card differs from a model card by covering…
choices: The whole application: prompts, tools, guardrails and oversight
quiz.why: Behavior depends on the system, not just the model.

quiz.q: "Open weights" licenses may still…
choices: Restrict commercial use or user counts
quiz.why: Read each license; terms vary widely.

lesson.intuition: In regulated deals, documents are part of the system. A model card says what a model is for, how it was evaluated and where it fails. A license says what you may do with it. Procurement documents say who processes your data and how you can leave. Architects need these as much as diagrams, because missing paperwork can stop a launch.
how: Collect the model card and license for each model you use, and write a system card for your own application.
Summarize evals, known limitations and intended use in plain language.
Check licenses: API terms of service, open-weight licenses and any use restrictions.
Run procurement checks: subprocessors, security questionnaires, data return and exit clauses.
Keep a change log so documentation tracks model and prompt updates.
lesson.example: License check: a team wants to use an open-weight model in a commercial product. Its license allows commercial use but requires attribution and forbids use above a monthly-active-user threshold without a separate agreement. Legal confirms the product stays below the threshold and the UI adds the required attribution.
mistakes: Assuming that a model hosted on Hugging Face is under a permissive license.
Writing a system card at launch and never updating it.
No plan to export prompts, evals and data when changing vendors.
lesson.enterprise: A public-sector agency requires a system card for each AI service: purpose, data used, model versions, eval results by user group, human oversight and contact for complaints. Vendors that can't provide one are not shortlisted.
takeaways: Cards communicate purpose, evals and limits.
Read the license before the prototype becomes a product.
Plan the exit in the contract.
lesson.diagram:
flowchart LR
  M[Model] --> MC[Model card + license]
  APP[Your application] --> SC[System card]
  MC --> SC
  SC --> PROC[Procurement: subprocessors, security, exit]
  PROC --> GO[Approved for use]
  CHG[Changes] --> LOG[Change log] --> SC
lesson.diagramAlt: Diagram: a model's card and license feed your application's system card, which goes through procurement before approval; a change log keeps the system card current.

subjects.title: AI Product Management and Product Engineering for Agents
subjects.why: Agentic products fail more from wrong problem, wrong UX or wrong autonomy level than from wrong model.
subjects.explainer:
AI Product Managers and Product Engineers decide what the agent should do, for whom, how users stay in control, and how success is measured. Agent products need new product muscles: specifying behavior with eval sets (the eval is the spec), choosing the autonomy level per action (suggest, draft, act with approval, act autonomously), designing UX for uncertainty (showing sources, progress, confidence and easy correction), and pricing when each task has variable cost.

Metrics combine outcome (task completion, time saved, resolution rate), quality (eval pass rates, escalation and correction rates), trust (adoption, retention, override frequency) and economics (cost per task vs value per task). Product engineers prototype rapidly with real models and real data, run A/B tests and ship iteratively behind flags.

Common mistakes: chat as the default UI when a button would do; full autonomy on day one; no feedback capture; pricing per seat while costs scale per task.

Mental model: autonomy is a dial you earn with evidence, one action at a time.

resources.title: Google PAIR Guidebook
resources.why: Google PAIR's People + AI Guidebook: patterns for user needs, mental models, explainability, feedback and graceful failure in AI products.

resources.title: Microsoft HAX Toolkit (human-AI interaction guidelines)
resources.why: Microsoft HAX Toolkit: 18 human-AI interaction guidelines, a design library and a workbook for planning AI experiences responsibly.

resources.title: Lenny's Newsletter: AI product evals
resources.why: Lenny's Newsletter guest post on AI evals for PMs: move beyond vibe checks to error analysis, rubrics and LLM judges.

subjects.project: Write a product spec for an agent feature as an eval set (30 cases) plus an autonomy matrix per action. Prototype the UX with source display and one-click correction, define outcome/quality/trust/economics metrics, and design an A/B test with a guardrail metric.

topics.title: Specs as evals and autonomy design
topics.explainer: Replace vague requirements with examples: inputs, expected behaviors and unacceptable behaviors, which engineers turn into the eval suite. For each action the agent can take, choose an autonomy level based on reversibility, cost of error and user trust, and define the evidence needed to raise it, such as 98% approval rate over 500 reviewed actions. This makes progress toward autonomy a measurable roadmap rather than a leap of faith.

subtopics.title: Unacceptable behaviors list
subtopics.text: List behaviors that must never happen, such as promising refunds or sharing another customer's data, and test for them.

subtopics.title: Autonomy levels per action
subtopics.text: Different actions in one agent can have different autonomy, for example auto-tagging but human-approved refunds.

topics.title: UX for agents
topics.explainer: Good agent UX shows what the agent is doing and why: progress for long tasks, sources and citations, previews of actions before they happen, and easy undo or correction. Use structured UI where possible instead of free chat. Make handoff to a human seamless and preserve context. Capture feedback at the point of correction, because that data is gold for evals. Design for failure states as carefully as for success.

subtopics.title: Progress and transparency
subtopics.text: Show what the agent is doing step by step so users trust it and can stop it.

subtopics.title: Undo and correction
subtopics.text: Make it easy to undo an action or correct an answer, and capture corrections as feedback.

topics.title: Metrics, experiments and pricing
topics.explainer: Define a metric stack: outcome metrics for value, quality metrics from evals and corrections, trust metrics like adoption and override rates, and economic metrics such as cost per task versus value per task. Run A/B tests with guardrail metrics so a cheaper model that raises escalations is caught. Price to align with value and cost: per task, per outcome or hybrid, with usage limits that prevent loss-making customers.

subtopics.title: Cost vs value per task
subtopics.text: Compare model and tool cost per task with the value of the task to make sure each use is profitable.

subtopics.title: Outcome-based pricing
subtopics.text: Outcome-based pricing charges per resolved task, which aligns with value but exposes you to variable costs.

quiz.q: What is the best form of an agent product spec?
choices: A set of example cases that become the eval suite
quiz.why: Evals make behavior requirements concrete and testable.

quiz.q: Which factor most determines an action's autonomy level?
quiz.why: Irreversible, costly actions need more oversight.

quiz.q: Why include a guardrail metric in A/B tests?
choices: To catch harm (e.g. more escalations) while optimizing the primary metric
quiz.why: Guardrails prevent wins that hurt other outcomes.

lesson.intuition: Product management for agents is about deciding what the agent should do, how much it is allowed to do on its own, and how users stay in control. The best AI PMs write specs as examples and evals, design UX that shows sources and progress, and start agents at low autonomy, raising it only when evidence shows it is safe.
how: Write the spec as examples: good outputs, bad outputs and unacceptable behaviors, then turn them into an eval set.
Choose an autonomy level per action: suggest, draft, act with approval, act autonomously.
Design UX for uncertainty: show sources, progress, confidence and easy undo or correction.
Define metrics across outcome, quality, trust and economics.
Experiment with guardrails, and raise autonomy only when metrics clear agreed thresholds.
lesson.example: Raising autonomy with evidence: an email-triage agent drafts replies that agents approve. Over 4 weeks, 2,000 drafts are approved unchanged 94% of the time, edited 5% and rejected 1%. The team agrees to auto-send only for the 'order status' category, where approval-unchanged was 99.2% over 600 drafts, and keeps approval for everything else.
mistakes: Shipping a free-form chat box when a structured UI would be clearer and safer.
Giving the agent full autonomy on day one.
Measuring usage only, not whether tasks were completed correctly.
lesson.enterprise: A B2B software company prices its support agent per resolved ticket instead of per seat. Because each resolution has a variable model cost, the team tracks cost per resolution weekly and caps agent steps to protect margins.
takeaways: The eval set is the spec.
Autonomy is earned per action with evidence.
Show your work: sources, progress, undo.
lesson.diagram:
flowchart LR
  SPEC[Examples + unacceptable behaviors] --> EV[Eval set]
  EV --> AUT{Autonomy level}
  AUT --> S1[Suggest]
  AUT --> S2[Draft]
  AUT --> S3[Act with approval]
  AUT --> S4[Act autonomously]
  S3 -->|evidence| S4
  S1 --> MET[Metrics: outcome, quality, trust, cost]
lesson.diagramAlt: Diagram: example-driven specs become an eval set that informs the autonomy level, from suggest to act autonomously, with evidence moving actions up and metrics tracking results.

case.title: Klarna AI assistant handles two-thirds of customer service chats in its first month (press release, Feb 2024)
case.summary: Klarna reported that its OpenAI-powered assistant had 2.3 million conversations in its first month, two-thirds of its customer service chats, doing work it equated to 700 full-time agents. It reported customer satisfaction on par with human agents, a 25% drop in repeat inquiries, and resolution in under 2 minutes versus 11 minutes before, in 23 markets and more than 35 languages.
case.lesson: Product teams should define the outcome metrics up front (resolution time, repeat contacts, satisfaction) and report them against the human baseline. These are company-reported figures, so treat them as a claim to compare against, not an independent benchmark.

# Product metrics for an agent, computed from conversation outcomes.
convos = [
  {"resolved": True,  "escalated": False, "minutes": 1.5, "repeat_within_7d": False},
  {"resolved": True,  "escalated": False, "minutes": 2.0, "repeat_within_7d": True},
  {"resolved": False, "escalated": True,  "minutes": 6.0, "repeat_within_7d": False},
  {"resolved": True,  "escalated": False, "minutes": 1.0, "repeat_within_7d": False},
]
n = len(convos)
print("resolution rate", sum(c["resolved"] for c in convos)/n)
print("escalation rate", sum(c["escalated"] for c in convos)/n)
print("repeat-contact rate", sum(c["repeat_within_7d"] for c in convos)/n)
print("avg handle minutes", sum(c["minutes"] for c in convos)/n)

subjects.title: Change Management, Adoption and Stakeholder Communication
subjects.why: A deployed assistant nobody uses has zero ROI. Adoption is designed: champions, training, workflow fit, feedback loops and steady communication with every stakeholder.
subjects.explainer:
AI changes how people work, so it triggers the usual change dynamics (fear of replacement, distrust, habit) plus new ones (unpredictable outputs, unclear accountability). Change models help structure the work. Prosci's ADKAR (Awareness, Desire, Knowledge, Ability, Reinforcement) looks at the individual; Kotter's 8 steps look at the organisation.

In practice: embed the tool in the existing workflow rather than a new tab, recruit champions in each team, train with real tasks, make feedback one click, publish what changed because of feedback, and measure usage and outcomes by team. Communicate on a rhythm: weekly to the working team, monthly to sponsors, and with clear messages about what the AI does and doesn't do.

resources.title: Prosci: The ADKAR Model
resources.why: Prosci's research-based individual change model (Awareness, Desire, Knowledge, Ability, Reinforcement), used to diagnose where people are stuck.

resources.title: Kotter: The 8-Step Process for Leading Change
resources.why: John Kotter's organisational change framework, from creating a sense of urgency and building a guiding coalition to anchoring new approaches in the culture.

resources.title: Microsoft HAX Toolkit
resources.why: Guidelines for human-AI interaction (set expectations, support correction, explain behaviour) that directly affect whether users trust and adopt an assistant.

resources.title: OpenAI: Morgan Stanley customer story
resources.why: How Morgan Stanley reached over 98% adoption among advisor teams, with evals, human review of outputs and clear data-use commitments building trust.

subjects.project: Write an adoption plan for an AI assistant rolling out to 400 support agents: stakeholder map with messages, champion network, training plan, in-workflow feedback, an adoption dashboard and a 90-day communication calendar.

topics.title: Designing for adoption
topics.explainer: People adopt tools that make their day easier and that they trust. Put the AI where work already happens (inside the ticketing tool, CRM or IDE), not in a separate portal. Explain clearly what it does, where it's weak, and that the human stays accountable. Recruit champions, respected peers who get early access and help shape the tool. Train with real scenarios from the users' own queue. Address job-security fears directly with leadership messaging about how roles will change. Use ADKAR to diagnose stalls: low usage with high awareness often means low ability (training) or low reinforcement (no follow-up).

subtopics.title: In-workflow placement
subtopics.text: Embed AI in the tools people already use; every extra click costs adoption.

subtopics.title: Champions network
subtopics.text: Respected peers in each team get early access, give feedback and coach colleagues.

subtopics.title: Training with real tasks
subtopics.text: Short, hands-on sessions using the team's own cases beat generic demos.

subtopics.title: ADKAR diagnosis
subtopics.text: Find which stage (awareness, desire, knowledge, ability or reinforcement) is the bottleneck for each group.

topics.title: Stakeholder communication and feedback loops
topics.explainer: Different stakeholders need different messages. Executives want outcomes against the business case. Process owners want workflow impact and risks. Users want 'what's in it for me' and how to get help. Security and legal want evidence of control. Set a cadence: a weekly working-team update, a monthly steering readout with metrics, and release notes users actually see. Close the loop on feedback: thumbs-down and comments become triaged issues, fixes ship, and you tell users what changed because of them. Report adoption honestly, broken down by team, along with the outcome metrics; vanity totals hide where the rollout is failing.

subtopics.title: Stakeholder-specific messages
subtopics.text: Outcomes for executives, workflow for owners, benefits and help for users, controls for risk teams.

subtopics.title: Communication cadence
subtopics.text: Weekly team updates, monthly steering readouts and visible release notes.

subtopics.title: Closing the feedback loop
subtopics.text: Triage feedback, ship fixes and announce 'you said, we did'.

subtopics.title: Adoption metrics by segment
subtopics.text: Active users, usage per task and outcome metrics by team, not just totals.

quiz.q: Usage is high in two teams and near zero in three others with the same tool. First step?
choices: Segment metrics by team and interview users to find the ADKAR bottleneck
quiz.why: Diagnose why each group is stuck before acting.

quiz.q: Where should a new AI assistant live for support agents?
choices: Inside the ticketing tool they already use
quiz.why: In-workflow placement removes friction.

quiz.q: What turns user feedback into trust?
choices: Visibly shipping fixes and telling users what changed because of their feedback
quiz.why: Closing the loop shows feedback matters.

lesson.intuition: Rolling out AI is like introducing a new colleague. People need to know what the newcomer is good at, where they make mistakes, and who's still responsible. They warm up faster when respected teammates vouch for them, and when their complaints visibly change how the newcomer works.
how: Map stakeholders and what each needs to hear.
Embed the tool in existing workflows; recruit champions per team.
Train with real tasks; set clear expectations about limits and accountability.
Instrument usage and outcomes by team; diagnose stalls with ADKAR.
Run a steady communication cadence and close every feedback loop.
lesson.example: Rollout to 400 agents in 4 waves of 100. Wave 1 has 12 champions. Week-2 dashboards show 85% weekly active users in two teams but 20% in the night shift. Interviews reveal the night shift was never trained (knowledge) and the tool times out on their VPN (ability). After training and a fix, night-shift usage reaches 70% by week 6. Monthly steering readouts track handle time, down from 9.5 to 7.8 minutes, alongside CSAT.
mistakes: Launching in a separate portal no one opens.
Measuring adoption only as a company-wide total.
Ignoring job-security concerns instead of addressing them openly.
Collecting feedback but never showing what changed.
lesson.enterprise: An insurer's claims copilot sat at 15% usage after launch. Moving it into the claims system's side panel, naming champions per office and publishing monthly 'you said, we did' notes raised weekly use to 72% in a quarter, and the steering committee extended funding.
takeaways: Adoption is designed, not announced.
Embed AI in existing workflows and use champions.
Segment adoption metrics and diagnose with ADKAR.
Communicate on a cadence and close feedback loops visibly.

flowchart LR
  SM["Stakeholder map + messages"] --> PL["Pilot wave with champions"]
  PL --> TR["Training on real tasks"]
  TR --> USE["In-workflow usage"]
  USE --> FB["One-click feedback"]
  FB --> FIX["Fixes shipped"]
  FIX --> NOTE["You said, we did"]
  NOTE --> USE
  USE --> DASH["Adoption + outcome dashboard by team"]
  DASH --> ST["Monthly steering readout"]
lesson.diagramAlt: Adoption loop: a stakeholder map leads to a pilot wave with champions, training on real tasks and in-workflow usage. One-click feedback becomes shipped fixes announced as 'you said, we did', feeding back into usage. Usage feeds an adoption and outcome dashboard by team, reported in a monthly steering readout.

case.title: Morgan Stanley uses AI evals to shape the future of financial services (OpenAI customer story)
case.summary: Morgan Stanley Wealth Management built an internal GPT-4 assistant for financial advisors and tested every AI use case with an evaluation framework before deployment, graded by advisors and prompt engineers. Daily regression tests of sample questions supported compliance, and OpenAI's zero data retention policy addressed the question of whether firm data would train public models. The firm reports over 98% adoption among advisor teams, with document access rising from 20% to 80%.
case.lesson: Evals plus clear answers to the data-use question are what move a pilot through risk review to firm-wide use. Adoption follows trust.

subjects.title: Measuring Business Impact and ROI
subjects.why: Budgets for AI renew on evidence. A baseline, a credible comparison and a cost model turn 'users like it' into a business case.
subjects.explainer:
ROI starts before the build: capture a baseline of the metric you'll move (handle time, resolution rate, cycle time, error rate) and its current cost. After launch, compare against that baseline credibly: ideally with a randomized holdout or A/B test, otherwise a staggered rollout or a matched comparison group, and be explicit about seasonality and other confounders. Value is translated into money (hours saved × loaded cost, revenue retained, errors avoided) and weighed against total cost of ownership: model and infrastructure spend, licences, people, integration and ongoing operations.

Report ranges and guardrails (quality, CSAT, risk), not just a headline number.

resources.title: Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments (Kohavi, Tang, Xu)
resources.why: The practical guide to A/B tests and holdouts from experimentation leaders at Microsoft, Google and LinkedIn: metrics, pitfalls and trustworthy analysis.

resources.title: GitHub: Quantifying Copilot's impact on developer productivity
resources.why: A randomized controlled experiment with 95 developers showing a 55% faster task completion with a confidence interval. A model for credible AI impact measurement.

resources.title: FinOps Foundation: FinOps for AI
resources.why: How to manage AI costs and tokenomics, allocate spend and build unit economics, which are the cost side of the ROI model.

resources.title: Klarna: AI assistant handles two-thirds of customer service chats
resources.why: Company-reported before/after metrics (resolution time, repeat inquiries, estimated profit impact). A useful example of the metrics an ROI readout uses.

subjects.project: Build an ROI model and measurement plan for an AI support assistant: baseline from 8 weeks of ticket data, a 10% holdout design, value and TCO calculations, sensitivity analysis and a one-page executive readout.

topics.title: Baselines and credible comparisons
topics.explainer: Without a baseline, every number is an anecdote. Before launch, record the outcome metric and its variation over several weeks, plus guardrails such as CSAT, accuracy and escalation rate. The strongest comparison is a randomized holdout: a share of users or tickets stays without AI, so seasonality affects both groups equally. If that isn't possible, use a staggered rollout (teams switch on at different times) or a difference-in-differences comparison against similar teams. Run long enough to cover weekly cycles and novelty effects, and report confidence intervals. Measure outcomes, not usage; usage is an input.

subtopics.title: Baseline before launch
subtopics.text: Several weeks of the target and guardrail metrics, with their natural variance.

subtopics.title: Randomized holdout or A/B
subtopics.text: Keep a control group without AI so trends and seasonality cancel out.

subtopics.title: Staggered rollout and diff-in-diff
subtopics.text: When randomization isn't possible, compare changes against similar untreated teams.

subtopics.title: Confidence intervals and duration
subtopics.text: Cover weekly cycles and novelty effects; report uncertainty, not just point estimates.

topics.title: Value, total cost and the business case
topics.explainer: Translate measured effects into money with explicit assumptions. Time saved × volume × loaded hourly cost gives capacity value; be honest about whether capacity is redeployed or actually reduces cost. Add revenue effects (conversion, retention) and avoided costs (errors, penalties) only with evidence. On the cost side, include model and API spend, infrastructure, vendor licences, build and integration effort, and ongoing run costs (evals, monitoring, support and content upkeep). Compute payback period and ROI, then run a sensitivity analysis on the two or three assumptions that matter most. Present a range and the guardrail metrics alongside the headline.

subtopics.title: Value translation
subtopics.text: Hours saved × loaded cost, revenue retained and errors avoided, each with a stated assumption.

subtopics.title: Total cost of ownership
subtopics.text: Tokens, infrastructure, licences, build, integration and ongoing operations.

subtopics.title: Payback and ROI
subtopics.text: Payback months = upfront cost ÷ monthly net benefit; ROI = (benefit − cost) ÷ cost.

subtopics.title: Sensitivity and guardrails
subtopics.text: Show how ROI moves with key assumptions, and report quality and risk metrics with it.

quiz.q: Handle time fell 15% after launch, but it also fell in a team without the tool. What does this suggest?
choices: Part of the drop is a trend or seasonal effect; compare against the control
quiz.why: Control groups separate the AI's effect from background change.

quiz.q: Which is an outcome metric rather than an input?
quiz.why: Usage and tokens are inputs; outcomes are what the business pays for.

quiz.q: Monthly net benefit is $40k and upfront cost is $200k. Payback period?

lesson.intuition: ROI is a before-and-after photo taken from the same angle, in the same light. The baseline is the 'before'. A control group makes sure the light didn't just change on its own. The cost model is the price tag. Executives trust the photo only if you show both pictures, how you took them, and the price.
how: Capture a multi-week baseline of outcome and guardrail metrics.
Design the comparison: randomized holdout, staggered rollout or diff-in-diff.
Measure outcomes over enough time and report confidence intervals.
Translate effects into money with explicit assumptions; build total cost of ownership.
Compute payback and ROI, run sensitivity analysis, and present a range plus guardrails.
lesson.example: Baseline: 42,000 tickets/month, 9.5 min average handle time, $38/hour loaded cost. With a 10% holdout over 8 weeks, AI-assisted tickets average 7.6 min versus 9.4 min in the holdout, a 1.8-minute (19%) effect, with a 95% CI of 1.4–2.2 min. Value: 37,800 assisted tickets × 1.8 min = 1,134 hours ≈ $43,100/month. Costs: $6,000/month for tokens and infrastructure plus $4,000/month to operate, so net ≈ $33,100/month. With $180k upfront, payback is about 5.4 months.
lesson.code:
import random, statistics, math
# Holdout-based effect estimate with a bootstrap CI, then value, TCO, payback and a sensitivity table.
rng = random.Random(42)
holdout = [max(1, rng.gauss(9.4, 3.0)) for _ in range(4_200)]     # minutes, tickets without AI
treated = [max(1, rng.gauss(7.6, 3.0)) for _ in range(37_800)]    # minutes, AI-assisted tickets
effect = statistics.mean(holdout) - statistics.mean(treated)
boots = sorted(statistics.mean(rng.choices(holdout, k=800)) - statistics.mean(rng.choices(treated, k=800)) for _ in range(2000))
lo, hi = boots[50], boots[1949]
print(f"effect {effect:.2f} min/ticket (95% CI ~{lo:.2f}-{hi:.2f})")
def roi(effect_min, tickets=37_800, loaded_hr=38.0, run_cost=10_000, upfront=180_000):
    value = tickets * effect_min / 60 * loaded_hr
    net = value - run_cost
    payback = upfront / net if net > 0 else math.inf
    return value, net, payback
v, net, pb = roi(effect)
print(f"value ${v:,.0f}/mo, net ${net:,.0f}/mo, payback {pb:.1f} months")
print("sensitivity (effect min -> payback months):")
for e in (lo, effect, hi):
    print(f"  {e:.2f} -> {roi(e)[2]:.1f}")
mistakes: No baseline before launch.
Attributing all improvement to AI without a control group.
Reporting usage (prompts, DAU) as impact.
Leaving ongoing run and people costs out of TCO.
lesson.enterprise: A telecom's steering committee had rejected two AI business cases built on vendor benchmarks. The third team ran a 10% randomized holdout for 8 weeks, reported a handle-time effect with confidence intervals, full TCO and a sensitivity table, and got approval to scale to all regions.
takeaways: Baseline first; no baseline, no ROI.
Use holdouts or staggered rollouts to isolate the AI's effect.
Measure outcomes, not usage.
Present value, full TCO, payback, sensitivity and guardrails together.

flowchart LR
  BL["Baseline (weeks before launch)"] --> EXP{"Comparison design"}
  EXP --> HO["Randomized holdout"]
  EXP --> ST["Staggered rollout / diff-in-diff"]
  HO --> EF["Effect + confidence interval"]
  ST --> EF
  EF --> VAL["Value: hours x cost, revenue, errors avoided"]
  TCO["TCO: tokens, infra, licences, build, ops"] --> ROI["ROI, payback, sensitivity"]

lesson.diagramAlt: A baseline captured before launch feeds a comparison design, either a randomized holdout or a staggered rollout with difference-in-differences, producing an effect with a confidence interval. The effect becomes value, which combines with total cost of ownership into ROI, payback and sensitivity, presented in an executive readout with guardrail metrics.

case.title: Klarna AI assistant handles two-thirds of customer service chats in its first month (press release, Feb 2024)
case.summary: Klarna reported its AI assistant's first-month impact against its prior human baseline: 2.3 million conversations (two-thirds of customer service chats), work it equated to 700 full-time agents, customer satisfaction on par with human agents, a 25% drop in repeat inquiries, and errands resolved in under 2 minutes versus 11 before. It estimated a $40 million profit improvement in 2024.
case.lesson: An ROI readout pairs volume and speed gains with quality guardrails (satisfaction, repeat contacts) and a money estimate. Treat company-reported figures as claims and build your own controlled measurement.

subjects.title: Sovereign & Regulated Architectures
subjects.why: Governments and banks pay for in-boundary designs.
subjects.explainer:
Sovereign AI keeps weights, logs, and often embeddings inside a boundary. Confidential GPUs/TEEs, air-gapped MLOps, signed supply chains, and offline red-team processes appear. Update channels become sneakernet or heavily controlled mirrors.

Common mistake: 'private VPC endpoint to a public model' sold as sovereign. Another: no patch story for CVEs in the serving stack.

Design evidence packs auditors can consume without a live demo.
