topics.title: Controls

subtopics.title: Confidential computing / TEEs
subtopics.text: Trusted execution environments encrypt data in use and can prove (attest) what code is running, including on some modern GPUs.

subtopics.title: Signed model supply chain
subtopics.text: Sign model files and containers and verify signatures before deployment so tampered artifacts are rejected.

topics.explainer: Sovereign and regulated deployments keep weights, prompts, logs and embeddings inside a legal and physical boundary. Confidential computing and GPU TEEs protect data in use from the cloud operator. Evals and red-teaming run inside the boundary too. Models arrive through a signed supply chain with verified hashes. Embedding and search run locally so documents never leave. A private network link to a public model API does not satisfy these requirements on its own.

topics.title: Operations

subtopics.title: Signed updates / sneakernet
subtopics.text: In air-gapped sites, updates arrive on approved media after scanning and signature checks, so plan update cycles in advance.

subtopics.title: Telemetry without exfil
subtopics.text: Monitoring must report health and metrics without sending prompts or data outside the boundary.

topics.explainer: Operating inside a boundary changes daily work. Updates arrive as signed bundles, sometimes physically carried in. Break-glass access for emergencies is logged and time-limited. Telemetry must be designed so metrics leave but data does not. Auditors expect evidence packs. Field support may require cleared staff on site, so the support model is part of the architecture, not an afterthought. Try it: write the runbook for a model update that must cross an air gap, from vendor release to signed bundle to production.

quiz.q: A public-model Private Link alone…
choices: Does not make processing fully sovereign
quiz.why: Data still leaves the boundary to the provider.

quiz.q: Confidential computing on GPUs protects data…
choices: In use, even from the host operator
quiz.why: TEEs encrypt memory and attest the environment.

quiz.q: In an air-gapped site, model updates typically arrive as…
quiz.why: Signatures and hashes protect the offline supply chain.

lesson.intuition: Sovereign AI keeps everything inside a boundary that a government, bank or regulator controls: the model weights, the data, the logs and often the people who can access them. It is more than picking a local region. It means you can run, update, monitor and audit the system without data or control leaving the boundary.
how: Define the boundary: country, cloud, data center or air-gapped network, and who may operate inside it.
Host weights, indexes, logs and embeddings inside the boundary, often on open-weight models.
Use confidential computing (TEEs) where operators must not see data in use.
Control the supply chain: signed model artifacts, mirrored package repositories, scanned containers.
Plan operations: controlled updates, break-glass access, telemetry that doesn't exfiltrate data, and auditor evidence packs.
lesson.example: Capacity planning in-boundary: a ministry expects 2,000 users at a peak of 0.2 requests per second total per 100 users, so about 4 requests per second. With an average 800 output tokens per request, that is 3,200 output tokens per second. If one GPU node sustains 2,000 output tokens per second for the chosen model, plan for 2 nodes plus 1 spare for N+1 redundancy.
mistakes: Selling a private endpoint to a foreign-hosted model as 'sovereign'.
No patch process for vulnerabilities in the serving stack inside an air gap.
Telemetry that sends prompts to an external vendor.
lesson.enterprise: A defense agency runs an open-weight model on GPUs in its own facility, imports updates only as signed bundles through a controlled transfer process, and keeps all logs on site. Auditors receive an evidence pack with hashes of every deployed artifact.
takeaways: Sovereign means operated and controlled in-boundary, not just hosted nearby.
Signed artifacts and controlled updates are essential.
Plan capacity with redundancy because you can't burst to a public cloud.

flowchart LR
  subgraph B[Sovereign boundary]
    W[Open weights] --> SRV[Serving]
    IDX[(Local index)] --> SRV
    SRV --> LOG[(Local logs)]
    TEE[Confidential compute] -.-> SRV
  end
  EXT[External updates] -->|signed bundle| MIR[Mirror / scanner] --> W
lesson.diagramAlt: Diagram: inside a sovereign boundary, open weights, a local index, serving, local logs and confidential compute; external updates enter only as signed bundles through a mirror and scanner.

subjects.title: Org Design & AI Transformation
subjects.why: Architecture without operating model fails at handoff.
subjects.explainer:
CoE versus federated versus hub-spoke, platform versus product teams, RACI for model incidents, and hiring skills matrices determine whether designs live. Pilots need explicit scale criteria; vendor sprawl needs governance; executives need metrics beyond demo wow.

Common mistake: centralizing all AI in a team that becomes a bottleneck. Another: federating with zero shared eval standards.

Team Topologies-style thinking maps cleanly onto AI platforms.

topics.title: Operating Models

subtopics.title: CoE vs federated vs hub-spoke
subtopics.text: A CoE centralizes expertise; federated teams build independently; hub-and-spoke mixes central standards with distributed delivery.

subtopics.title: RACI for incidents
subtopics.text: RACI says who is Responsible, Accountable, Consulted and Informed for each decision or incident type.

topics.explainer: Organizations typically pick a Center of Excellence (central experts), a federated model (each business unit builds), or hub-and-spoke (central platform plus embedded builders). Separate the platform team, which provides paved roads, from product teams, which ship features. Write a RACI for AI incidents. Keep a skills matrix so you know who can do evals, infra, security and domain review. Manage vendors centrally to avoid twenty contracts with the same provider.

topics.title: Change

subtopics.title: Pilot to scale criteria
subtopics.text: Agree in advance what evidence a pilot needs to scale, so decisions aren't driven by demos.

subtopics.title: Shadow IT risk
subtopics.text: When official tools are slow or missing, people use personal accounts. Provide a good sanctioned option quickly.

topics.explainer: Pilots are easy; scaling is hard. Define criteria to graduate a pilot: measured quality, cost per task, security review, owner on call. Watch for shadow AI, where teams use unapproved tools because the official path is slow. Control sprawl by consolidating gateways and prompt stores. Report executive metrics in business terms such as hours saved or resolution rate, and invest in training so staff know what the tools can and cannot do.

quiz.q: A platform team should…
choices: Provide golden paths and reduce cognitive load
quiz.why: Platforms enable; they do not bottleneck forever.

quiz.q: Hub-and-spoke AI organizations combine…
choices: A central platform with builders embedded in business units
quiz.why: The hub provides paved roads; spokes ship domain features.

quiz.q: A good criterion to graduate a pilot is…
choices: Measured quality, cost per task, security review and an on-call owner
quiz.why: Scale needs evidence and ownership.

lesson.intuition: Great architectures fail if the organization around them doesn't work. Someone has to own models, evals, incidents and vendor choices. Companies usually move from a central AI team, to a hub that sets standards while product teams build, as skills spread. The architect helps design that operating model so designs survive handover.
how: Choose an operating model: central center of excellence, federated teams, or hub-and-spoke.
Split responsibilities: a platform team for shared services, product teams for use cases.
Define RACI for model incidents, eval standards and vendor approval.
Set pilot-to-scale criteria and track a portfolio of use cases with executive metrics.
Invest in training and a skills matrix so teams can own their AI features.
lesson.example: Pilot-to-scale gate: a pilot moves to scale only if it meets (1) its eval threshold on the golden set, (2) at least 30% weekly active use among target users for four weeks, (3) cost per task within budget, and (4) security and privacy sign-off. Of 12 pilots in a year, a company scales 4 and stops 8, freeing budget early.
mistakes: A central AI team that becomes a bottleneck for every request.
Federating to many teams with no shared eval or security standards.
Counting pilots launched instead of outcomes delivered.
lesson.enterprise: A bank runs a hub-and-spoke model: the hub owns the gateway, eval standards and vendor list; business units build their own assistants on top. A monthly review shows each use case's adoption, quality and cost to executives.
takeaways: Ownership is architecture too.
Hub sets standards, spokes deliver value.
Gate pilots on evidence, then scale or stop.

case.title: Research: quantifying GitHub Copilot's impact on developer productivity and happiness (2022)
case.summary: In a controlled experiment, 95 professional developers were randomly split into two groups to write an HTTP server in JavaScript. The Copilot group finished 55% faster (1 h 11 min vs 2 h 41 min, P = .0017, 95% CI 21–89%). Completion rate was 78% vs 70%.
case.lesson: Measure AI transformation with controlled comparisons and confidence intervals, not anecdotes. Note the wide interval even for a strong effect.
